**(p-202)** Surat al-Kahf (The Cave) is Meccan, except for verses twenty-eight, and from verse eighty-three to verse one hundred and one, which are Medinan. Its verses number one hundred and ten.

﴿Praise belongs to God, who sent down upon His servant﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ) ﴿the Book﴾. That is, the complete Book, which is free from any imperfection, known for this perfection among the books, and deserving that the name "Book" be exclusively applied to it. It refers to the whole Qur'an, or to all that was sent down at that time, as has been mentioned repeatedly. The description of God with the relative clause (al-mawsul) implies that what is in the clause is the reason for deserving praise, and it announces the great status of this glorious revelation. How could it not? For upon it revolves the orbit of happiness in both abodes. In referring to the Messenger (ﷺ) as "the servant," in apposition to the pronoun of Majesty (al-jalala), there is an alert to his (ﷺ) reaching the highest ascents of worship, and an honouring of him, what an honour! It also implies that it is the nature of a messenger to be a servant of the one who sent him, unlike what the Christians claimed concerning Jesus, peace be upon him. The explicit object is placed after the prepositional phrase, although its proper place is before it, so that the words ﴿and not made in it any crookedness﴾ may be joined to it. That is, not any crookedness, by way of some disorder in the composition or contradiction in meaning. Or, it has deviated from calling to the truth; and this, in meanings, is like crookedness in physical things. As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿You will not see in it any crookedness or curvature﴾, although the mountains are among physical things, it is to indicate the negation of crookedness that is not perceived by the sense of sight, but is rather known only through insight, by means of the use of geometric measures. And since that is not perceived by the apparent senses, it is counted among what belongs to meanings. It has been said: the vowel fatha in ﴿عِوَجًا﴾ (ʿiwajan) is used for crookedness in what stands upright, such as a stick or a wall, while the kasra (ʿiwajan with kasra on the first letter, i.e., ʿiwaj) is used for crookedness in other than that, whether physical or abstract.

﴿Qayyiman﴾ (upright), watching over the religious and worldly welfare of the servants, as indicated by what follows of warning and good tidings. In that case it is a description of Him as perfecting after the description of Him as perfect. Or it refers to what came before it of the heavenly Books, bearing witness to their soundness and watching over them (muhaymin). Or it means extremely straight, in which case it is an emphasis on what the negation of crookedness indicates, together with the benefit that this is among His essential, necessary attributes, as the form (al-sigha) indicates, and not that crookedness was negated from it while it was among its possible qualities. Its being in the accusative (intisab) is on the assumption that the preceding sentence is conjoined to the relative clause (sila) by an implied verb indicated by the negation of crookedness, its estimate being: He made it upright (ja'alahu qayyiman). As for the assumption that it is circumstantial (hāliyya), then it is in the circumstantial state of "the Book," since in that case there is no separation whereby parts of the conjoined element are divided by the conjoining element. It is also read as "qiyaman" (qiyaman).

﴿Li-yundhira﴾ is connected to "anzala" (He sent down). The agent is the Divine Name (the pronoun of Majesty), as in the two verbs conjoined to it. The omission of mention of the first object is to signal that what the speech is directed toward is the second object, and that the first is evident and there is no need to mention it. That is: He sent down the Book so that He might warn, through what is in it, those who disbelieve in it.

﴿Ba's﴾, that is: punishment.

﴿Shadidan min ladunhu﴾, that is: issuing from Him, descending from His presence, in recompense for their disbelief and denial. It is also read as "min ladnihi" with the dal silent and the damma indicated (ishmam), the nun kasra due to the meeting of two silent letters, and the ha kasra for assimilation (itba').

﴿Wa-yubashshira﴾ with the shadda (intensive doubling). It is also read without the shadda.

﴿Al-mu'minin﴾, that is: those who affirm Him.

﴿Alladhina ya'malun al-salihat﴾ the righteous deeds that are explained within it. The choice of the present/future form (istiqbal) in the relative clause is to indicate the renewal and continuity of the righteous deeds, and the placing of the relative pronoun after its described antecedent mentioned is because the basis of the acceptance of deeds is faith.

﴿Anna lahum﴾, that is: that they have, in return for their faith and the deeds mentioned.

﴿Ajran hasanan﴾, which is Paradise, and what is in it of good rewards.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 3:

﴿ماكِثِينَ﴾ (*makithin*, "remaining") is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) from the pronoun in "لَهُمْ" (*lahum*, "for them"), which is in the genitive case.

﴿فِيهِ﴾ (*fihi*, "therein") means: in that reward.

﴿أبَدًا﴾ (*abadan*, "forever") means without end, that is, abiding in it eternally. It is in the accusative as a *zarfiyya* (adverbial accusative of time, indicating when or for how long the action occurs) modifying *makithin*. The placing of the warning before the glad tidings serves to show the utmost concern with restraining the disbelievers from what they are upon, while observing the principle of clearing away (*takhliya*, removing what is blameworthy) before adorning (*tahliya*, adorning with what is praiseworthy). The repetition of the warning is by His, may He be exalted, saying:

ﷺ

﴿And warn those who say, "Allah has taken to Himself a son."﴾ This is connected to a specific group from among those whom the preceding warning encompassed, namely those deserving of severe punishment, to indicate the utter horror of their state and the extreme ugliness of their disbelief and error. That is, "And warn, from among all the disbelievers, these particular ones who utter such a monstrous saying specifically." They are the disbelievers of the Arabs who say, "The angels are the daughters of Allah, the Exalted," the Jews who say, "'Uzayr (Ezra) is the son of Allah," and the Christians who say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah."

Leaving the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "the relative clause") unattached to its antecedent (al-mawsuf), as was done in His saying, "and give glad tidings to the believers," serves to indicate that what lies within the relative clause (al-silah) is sufficient to establish their disbelief in the most odious manner. The choice of the past tense form (sigha al-madi) in the relative clause serves to show the certain occurrence of that abominable utterance from them in what is being recounted. Making the omitted object in the preceding verb refer to this group would lead to the exclusion of all other categories of disbelievers from the warning and threat. The generalization of the warning there to the believers too, by understanding it in the sense of mere informing of a harmful report without considering the arrival of what is warned of upon the one warned, as in His saying, ﴿that you may warn the people and give glad tidings to those who believe﴾, would result in the noble composition being devoid of indicating that severe punishment befalls anyone other than this group.

It is also permissible that the subject in the three verbs be the pronoun referring to the Book, or the pronoun referring to the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿Of it they have no knowledge﴾, that is, of their taking to Himself, glorified and exalted be He, a son.

﴿Knowledge﴾ (ʿilm) is in the nominative, either as the subject (mubtada') or as the agent (fāʿil) because the prepositional phrase precedes it and relies on it. The ﴿min﴾ (from) is extra (mazīdah), for emphasis of the negation. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah) or a resumed clause (mustaʾnafah), explaining their state in their saying. That is: they have no knowledge of that whatsoever, not because they have failed to follow a method while the known object is established or possible, but because it is impossible in itself.

﴿Nor do their fathers﴾, who imitated them and so wandered together in the bewilderment of ignorance and error. Or it means: they have no knowledge of whether what they said is correct or mistaken. Rather, they said it by casting out a guess born of blindness and ignorance, without thought or deliberation, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And they invented for Him sons and daughters without knowledge﴾. Or it means: they have no knowledge of the reality of what they said, and of the great magnitude of its enormity, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Indeed you have produced something monstrous. The heavens are almost torn apart from it﴾ ... and the verses. This is the most suitable reading in light of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Grievous is the word﴾, that is, their saying is great in disbelief and fabrication, because in it they attribute to Him, glorified be He, what scarcely befits the majesty of His presence.

The agent of ﴿kabura﴾ (it is grievous) is either a pronoun referring to the saying, indicated by ﴿qālū﴾ (they say), and ﴿kalimatan﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz); or it is an ambiguous pronoun (ḍamīr mubham) explained by the indefinite accusative noun after it as a specification, as in ﴿niʿma rajulan﴾ (how excellent a man). The object of praise or blame that is omitted is supplied as: ﴿kabura hiya kalimatan kharijatan min afwāhihim﴾ (grievous is it, a word coming out of their mouths).

It is also read as ﴿kabrat﴾ with the ﹽ ba' sukun and with a faint indication of the ḍammah (ishmām). It is also read as ﴿kalimatun﴾ in the nominative. The clause ﴿takhruju min afwāhihim﴾ (coming out of their mouths) is a qualifier of the word, conveying the magnitude of their audacity in uttering it. The attribution of coming out to the word is made although what actually comes out is the air shaped by the form of sound, because it is connected to it.

﴿They speak only falsehood﴾. That is: they say, concerning that matter, nothing but a lying saying that does not at all fall within the possibility of truth. The two pronouns refer to them and to their fathers. It is like the state of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his intense grief over the people's turning away and their refusal to believe in the Qur'an, and his complete sorrow for them, being like one who is expected to destroy himself upon losing what he loves when parting from his beloved, out of regret at their departure and longing for them at their migration. It has been said that this is in the manner of a figurative expression (ṭarīqat al-tamthīl), taking it that he (ﷺ) was being told to be cautious and concerned about this.

**﴿So perhaps you would destroy yourself﴾** means: **﴿over their traces﴾**, out of grief and longing at their separation from you. It is also read as **﴿بِالإضافَةِ﴾** (bi-l-idafa, "with the genitive construction"), that is, as *nafsaka* ("your self") rather than *nafsaka* as a separate object.

**﴿if they do not believe in this discourse﴾** means the Qur'an, which the surah refers to at its beginning as "the Book." The apodosis of the conditional is omitted, relying on what precedes it as evidence of its meaning. It is also read with **أنِ** (*an*, with the fatha), meaning "because they do not believe." In that reading, the governing of **باخِعٌ** (*bakhi'un*, "destroying") is taken as a narration of a past state, to bring the scene vividly before the mind, as in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿stretching out his two forearms﴾ (Qur'an 18:18).

**﴿أسَفًا﴾** (*asafan*, "in sorrow") is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) for **باخِعٌ**, meaning: because of the intensity of grief and anger. Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the pronoun within the word, meaning: "being sorrowful over them."

It is permissible to read the noble verse as a **استعارة تبعية** (*isti'ara tab'iyya*, a metaphor in which the figurative term is a verb, participle, or other derived form, so that the comparison is between the parts of the two sides rather than between the two whole situations drawn from them), as opposed to a **تمثيل** (*tamthil*, an allegorical image in which the comparison is between two whole situations). Its verification has already been discussed in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God has sealed their hearts﴾ (Qur'an 2:7).

﴿Indeed, We have made what is upon the earth﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) and an explanation (*ta'lil*) of the sense of apprehension (*al-ishfaq*) contained in *la'alla*. That is: Indeed, We have made what is upon it, of the adornments, from among those other than those to whom the obligation (*taklif*) is addressed, whether animal, plant, or mineral, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾.

﴿Adornment﴾ is the second object of *al-ja'l* (making) if it is taken in the sense of *al-tasyir* (transforming into), or a circumstantial state (*hal*) if it is taken in the sense of *al-ibda'* (originating). The *lam* in ﴿for it﴾ is either related to *zinatan* (adornment), or to an omitted element that is a qualifier of it, meaning: existing for it, that is, so that those among the obligated who look upon it may enjoy it and benefit from it by contemplation and inference. Indeed, serpents and scorpions, insofar as they remind one of the punishment of the Hereafter, are among the benefits. Rather, every created thing falls under the adornment insofar as it indicates the existence of the Maker and His oneness. Indeed, spouses and children are also among the adornments of the worldly life, rather the greatest of them. This does not prevent them from being among the obligated, for in respect of their connection to their companions they fall under the adornment, and in respect of being obligated they fall under the trial (*ibtila'*).

﴿That He may test them﴾ is connected to *ja'alna* (We made), meaning: We made what We made in order to deal with them in the manner of one who tests them.

﴿Which of them is best in deed﴾: so that We may recompense them with reward and punishment, as is distinguished the good-doer from the evil-doer, and the classes of individuals of each of the two groups become distinguished according to the distinction of the ranks of their knowledge, which are arranged in their perceptions, and the differences in the degrees of their deeds that branch from that, as we have established at the beginning of Surat Hud.

*Ayyu* (which) may be an interrogative (*istifhamiyya*), in the nominative by inception (*mubtada'*), with *ahsanu* (best) as its predicate (*khabar*), and the clause is in the place of the accusative, suspending the verb of trial (*mu'allaqa li-fi'l al-balwa*) because it carries the sense of knowledge in respect of its outcome, like questioning and considering; for this reason it has been treated as such by way of illustration (*tamthil*) or figurative extension (*isti'ara tab'iyya*). Or it may be a relative pronoun (*mawsula*) meaning *alladhi* (the one who), with *ahsanu* as the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is a relative clause (*sila*) for it, and it is in the accusative position as a substitute (*badal*) for the object of *li-nabluwahum*, the estimated meaning being: that We may test him who is best in deed. In that case, the *damma* in *ayyuhum* may be a fixed vowel (*lil-bina'*), as in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Then We will certainly draw out from every sect whichever of them is most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾, according to one of the opinions, since the condition for fixed vowel, which is the annexation (*idafa*) in form, is fulfilled, and the initial part of the relative clause is omitted. It may also be for inflection (*i'rab*), because what has been mentioned is a condition for the permissibility of fixed vowel, not its obligation.

The goodness of deed consists in asceticism regarding the world, not being deceived by it, contentment with little of it, spending it as it ought to be spent, reflecting on its state, making it a means (*dhari'a*) to knowing its Creator, enjoying it to the extent permitted by the Law, fulfilling its rights, and being thankful for it, and not taking it as a means to lusts and corrupt aims, as the disbelievers and the people of whims do.

The use of the superlative form, although the trial includes both groups in respect of their deeds, which are divided into good and evil and not merely into good and better, is to indicate that the original purpose of the aforementioned making is only the manifestation of the perfection of the goodness of the good-doers, as has been verified in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾.

"And indeed We will make" — what will come, when the life of the world reaches its end — "that which is upon it" of creatures, all of them, by annihilating them entirely. The expression "that which is upon it" is stated in the form of a pronoun-reference rather than a noun-form only to add emphasis, or to include the responsible beings (al-mukallafun) within it.

"Ṣaʿīdan" (a smooth, bare ground, sometimes glossed as dust or the surface of the earth) is the second object of the verb "jaʿl" (to make). "Ṣaʿīd" means dust, or the surface of the earth. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is the level part of the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the road on which there is no vegetation.

"Juruzan" means dust with no vegetation in it, after it had been something whose beauty the onlookers marvel at, and whose sight the eyes take pride in beholding. It is said: "a land juruz" means a land with no vegetation in it, and "a year juruz" means a year without rain. Al-Farra' said: the land was "juruzat," so it is "majruzah," meaning its vegetation has gone away due to drought or locusts. It is also said: locusts, sheep and camels "jaraza" it when they eat what is upon it. This sentence serves to complete the reasoning given in the preceding clause. The meaning: do not grieve over what you witness from the people, of their denial of what We have sent down to you of the Book, for We have made what is upon the earth of various kinds of things an adornment for it, so that We may test their deeds, and then recompense them according to them. And indeed We will reduce all of that to nothing soon, and recompense them according to their deeds.

﴿Or did you think﴾ is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The intent is to deny that his community reckoned this. The "am" here is a disjunctive particle, interpreted as if preceded by "bal" (rather, nay), which is used for moving from one topic to another and not for negating what came before. Most scholars (al-Jumhur) read it with the interrogative hamzah, while others read "bal" alone. The meaning is: "Rather, did you reckon that the companions of the cave and the ar-Raqim were, in their remaining alive, for a long span of time?"

﴿among Our signs﴾: among Our signs, which include what We mentioned of making what is on the earth an adornment for it, for the wisdom already indicated, and then making all of that a barren, dusty ground, as though it had not flourished yesterday.

﴿a wonder﴾: that is, a sign of wonder. It is placed in the position of the genitive construction (idafah), or it is described as a verbal noun (masdar) for emphasis. It is the predicate of "kanu" (were). "Among Our signs" is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to it. The meaning is that their story, although it breaks customary norms, is not a marvel in comparison with the rest of the signs, which include what was mentioned of the wonders of Allah's creation. Rather, in their presence it is like a small, insignificant trifle.

The cave (al-kahf) is a wide cave in a mountain. The ar-Raqim is their dog. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"And there was not in it except al-Raqim, neighboring,
and their hunting dog, while the people in the cave lay motionless."

It is also said that the ar-Raqim is a lead or stone tablet on which their names were inscribed and which was placed at the entrance of the cave. It is said that it is the valley in which the cave lies, so it derives from "raqmat al-wadi," meaning its side. It is said that it is the mountain. It is said that it is their town. It is said that their place was between Ghadban and Ayla, short of Palestine. It is also said that the companions of the ar-Raqim are others, who were three, and the cave closed upon them, so they were saved by each of them mentioning the best of his deeds, as detailed in the two Sahih collections (al-Sahihayn, i.e., Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 10:

﴿Idh awā﴾ (when they took refuge) is an adverbial clause (ẓarf) governing ʿajaban, not laḥasibta; or it is an object (mafʿūl) of udhkur (remember), meaning: at the time when they took refuge.

﴿al-fityah﴾ (the youths) means the People of the Cave. The explicit noun was preferred over a pronoun in order to affirm the state of youthful nobility (futūwa) they had within themselves, for they were youths from among the nobles of the Romans, whom Diqyanus (Decius) compelled to idolatry, so they fled from him with their religion. And because the companionship of the Cave is a consequence of their taking refuge in the cave, it is not appropriate to consider it together with them before it is explained. ﴿ilā al-kahf﴾ (to the cave) in their mountain, for sitting, and they took it as a shelter.

﴿Fa-qālū rabbanā ātinā min ladunka﴾ (So they said: "Our Lord, grant us from Yourself"), that is, from the treasuries of Your special mercy, hidden from the eyes of the people of customary habits. Thus "min" is for origin (ibtidāʾiyya), connected to ātinā, or to an omitted element that occurred as a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from its second object, placed before it because it is indefinite; had it been postponed, it would have been a qualifier of it, meaning: grant us, coming from You.

﴿raḥmatan﴾ (mercy), special mercy that entails forgiveness, provision, and security from enemies.

﴿Wa-hayyi⁠ʾ lanā min amrinā﴾ (And prepare for us from our affair) — the affair in which we are, of emigrating from the disbelievers and persevering in Your obedience. The root meaning of tahyiʾa is bringing about the form (hayʾa) of a thing; that is: set right, arrange, and complete for us from our affair.

﴿rashadan﴾ (right guidance): reaching the path that leads to the desired goal, and being guided to it. Both prepositional phrases are connected to hayyiʾ, since their meanings differ. The fronting of the two prepositional phrases before the explicit object shows concern for them and highlights the desire for the postponed item, by placing first its circumstances; for postponing what deserves to come first, while placing before it what is among its desirable aspects, both creates the listener's longing for its arrival and indicates the speaker's complete desire for it and his concern that it be attained without fail. The same applies to the fronting of the phrase "min ladunka" (from You), on the assumption that it is connected to "ātinā", and the fronting of "lanā" (for us) before "min amrinā" (from our affair), to announce from the very beginning that what is asked for is desired by them. Or, make our affair entirely right guidance, with min being explicative (tajrīdiyya), similar to your saying: "I saw from you a lion."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 11:

﴿So We struck upon their ears﴾ i.e., We put them to sleep, by way of a figurative expression (tamthil) built upon likening the heavy sleep that prevents sounds from reaching the ears to a veil being cast over them. The singling out of the ears for mention, although all the senses share in being veiled from awareness during sleep, is because they are ordinarily the ones in need of veiling, since they are generally the means of waking, especially when the sleeper is alone and withdrawn from people. It was also said: "Striking upon the ears" is a metaphor (kinayah) for heavy sleep, and its being taken to mean their disabling (of hearing) is like the saying of people: "The governor struck upon the hand of the subjects," i.e., he prevented them from acting freely. However, this does not fit what comes later about the resurrection (al-ba'th), and it does not indicate sleep, though sleep is certainly what is meant.

The "fa" (then) in "fa-darabna" is like in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿fa-istajabna lahu﴾ (So We answered him), after His words, exalted is He: ﴿idh nada﴾ (when he called out). For the mentioned striking, and what followed from it of turning them to the right and to the left, and of resurrection, and other things, are a bestowal of mercy from Us (rahmatan min ladunna), hidden from the sight of those who cling to ordinary causes, in response to their supplication. ﴿In the cave﴾ (fi al-kahf) is a locative adverb for "darabna" (We struck). ﴿Years﴾ (sinin) is a temporal adverb for it, with respect to its duration rather than its beginning.

﴿Numbered﴾ ('adadan) i.e., possessing a number, or counted as a number; this is either as a verbal noun (masdar), or in the sense of a passive participle, "counted." The description of the years by this is either for magnification (lil-taksir), and this is more fitting with displaying the completeness of power; or for minimization (lil-taqlil), and this is more suitable to the context of denying that the story is a marvel among the other wondrous signs, since the length of their stay is like part of a day in His sight, Mighty and Majestic is He.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 18, verse 12:**

﴿Then We raised them﴾, that is, We awakened them from that heavy sleep, which resembled death.

﴿That We might know﴾, with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama). It was also read with the yā' (ya), in the active voice, by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person). In either case, it is a purpose (ghaya) of the raising. However, knowledge (al-'ilm) should not be taken as a metaphor for manifestation (al-idhar) and distinction (al-tamyiz). Nor should it be understood as something that can be a purpose of the raising by means of present knowledge, which is tied to the consequence, as in His saying: ﴿except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾, and His saying: ﴿and that Allah might know those who believe﴾, and similar examples in which knowledge is definitively realized through the realization of its object. The change of the qibla had the result of dividing people into followers and those who turned back. Likewise, the alternation of days among people had the result of dividing them into those who remained steadfast in faith and those who wavered in it. Both groups were the objects of present knowledge, manifestation, and distinction. As for the raising of these people, it did not result in their division into those who counted (al-muhsi) and others, such that knowledge or manifestation and distinction would be tied to them, nor could any of that be placed within the category of purpose. Rather, what resulted from it was their division into one who estimates by an inaccurate estimate and one who delegates to divine knowledge, and neither of these has anything to do with counting. Instead, the noble verse is to be understood as an illustration (tamthil) built upon making knowledge a metaphor for testing (al-ikhtibar), by way of applying the name of the effect to the cause. Testing does not necessarily require that the act by which one is tested be definitively carried out by the one being tested. It may be for the purpose of showing his incapacity to do it, in the manner of impossible commands (al-taklifat al-ta'jiziyya), as in His saying: ﴿so bring it from the west﴾, and this is what is meant here. The meaning, then, is: We raised them in order to deal with them as one who tests them.

﴿Which of the two parties﴾, that is, the two groups that differed concerning the length of their stay, by estimation and delegation, as will come later.

﴿Is more exact﴾, that is, more precise, ﴿in reckoning﴾, that is, in their stay (li-lubthihim), ﴿the term﴾, that is, the limit, so that their incapacity becomes manifest to them, and they delegate that matter to the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. And so that they might recognize their own condition and what Allah the Exalted did with them, by preserving their bodies and their religion, so that they would increase in certainty regarding the perfection of His power and knowledge, and would gain insight through it into the matter of resurrection. That would be a kindness (lutf) to the believers of their time and a clear sign to their unbelievers. Here, from those sublime ends, only their origin (mabda'ihā), which proceeds from Him, the Mighty and Majestic, is mentioned. As for what comes after, it refers to their questioning that led to these ends, which will come later. This is preferable to depicting the illustration by saying: "We raised them in the manner of one who wishes to know..." etc., as occurred in the explanation of His saying: "and that Allah might know those who believe" according to one of the views, where it was understood to mean "We did that in the manner of one who wishes to know who among the firm in faith is distinct from the one who is not firm", because it might be supposed from this that the wish entails the realization of the wished-for thing, and then the prohibited matter returns. Thus, one proceeds to making the wish to know a metaphor for testing: "test and choose." This has also been read as (liyu'lama) in the passive voice, and in the active voice from ilam (informing), on the basis that the first object is omitted, and the clause introduced by "ayyu" (which) occupies the position of the second object only, if knowledge is taken as cognitive (irfani). Or it occupies the position of the two objects if knowledge is taken as certain (yaqini), meaning: "that Allah might inform the people which of the two parties is more exact in reckoning..." etc.

Ibn 'Ata' narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that one of the two parties was the youths, and the other was the kings who ruled the city, one king after another. It was also said that both were from outside them. The first is more apparent, for the definite article (al-lam) indicates a known reference, and there is no known reference to anyone else. The word "amad" (term) means the same as "mada" (extent), like the word "ghaya" (limit) in their saying: "the beginning of the limit" and "the end of the limit". It is the object of "ahsa" (counted), and the prepositional phrase and its genitive is a circumstantial element (hal) from it, placed before it because it is indefinite. The meaning of counting that period is not to count it in terms of its continuous, intrinsic quantity, for that is not called counting. Rather, it is to count it in terms of its divided quantity, which is accidental to it, by considering its division into years, and reaching through that aspect the levels of numbers. This is what the fact that the period refers to the years mentioned before indicates. It is also permissible that "amad" be understood in its conventional meaning, with an elided modifier, that is: "for the time of their stay", and also without that. For the stay is an expression for a continuous state that corresponds to the mentioned time. Thus, by considering the extension that accidentally belongs to it because of this, it necessarily has a term. Yet the term is not what falls as the limit and end of that continuous state, considered in terms of its continuous quantity, which accidentally belongs to it because it corresponds to the extended time essentially. That is the moment of their awakening from their sleep, for knowing it from that aspect is not hidden from anyone, and it is not called counting, as has passed. Rather, considered in terms of its divided quantity, it is opposed to it, because those divisions accidentally belong to its time, which corresponds to it, by considering its division into years and its reaching a specific level of the levels of number, as has been verified in the first case. The difference between the two considerations is that what counting relates to in the earlier case is the period itself, divided into years, which is the total of three hundred and nine years. In the latter case, it is the endpoint of that period into which it is divided, namely the ninth year after the three hundred. The relation of counting to the term in the first sense is evident. As for its relation in the second sense, it is by considering its organizing what falls under it of levels of number, and its comprising them. This is according to the assumption that what is in His saying "for what they remained" is a verbal noun (masdariyya). It is also permissible that it be a relative pronoun (mawsula) whose returning pronoun is omitted from the relative clause, meaning: "for the duration in which they remained, which was expressed earlier as years in number." So "amad" is in its conventional meaning, as you have realized. It was also said: "the lam is superfluous (mazida), the relative is the object, and 'amadan' is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz)."

As for what was said, that "ahsa" is a superlative (ism al-tafdil), because it conforms to what occurs in other noble verses, such as ﴿which of them is best in deed﴾, ﴿which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾, and other examples that cannot be counted, and because its being a past verb indicates that the end of the raising is the knowledge of counting that precedes the raising, not the counting that comes after it, and that is not the case: the claim that the coming of the superlative from a derived form is not analogical is refuted by the fact that, according to Sibawayh, it is analogical in every case, and according to Ibn 'Usfur, in cases where its hamza is not for transference. There is no doubt that what we are dealing with belongs to that category. The prohibition of its operating is only with respect to other operated elements apart from the specification. As for the claim that the specification must be the subject in meaning, there is someone who can deny it, by the validity of saying: "which of them knows this verse best in meter or scansion?" Or it may be said: the operator for "amadan" is an elided verb indicated by the mentioned one, meaning: "he counts for what they remained a term," as in his saying:

*"And more striking among us with the swords were the helmets."*

The notion of falling into what is prohibited without benefit is refuted by what was pointed out regarding the benefit of conformity with similar cases. Together with what it contains of forcing and defect, it is far from correct, because its implication is that the purpose of the report would be to show the better of the two parties and to distinguish him from the lesser, while the basic act of counting is realized in both. It is clear that there is no realization of it at all, and that the purpose of the testing is to show the incapacity of all of them regarding it entirely. So it is definitively a past verb. The supposition that it indicates that the end of the raising is the knowledge of counting that precedes it is refuted by the fact that the past form is considered in terms of the state of narration. And Allah knows best.

(p-209) ﴿We relate to you their story in truth﴾. This begins the detailed account of what was summarized earlier in His words, Exalted is He: "When the youths took refuge in the cave..." etc. That is: We inform you of the details of their news. The derivation of this word has already been explained at the beginning of Surat Yusuf, peace be upon him.

﴿Their story (nabaʾahum)﴾: al-nabaʾ is news that has importance and gravity.

﴿In truth (bil-haqq)﴾: this may be an adjective of a omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in naqussu, or from nabaʾahum. Or it may be an adjective of it according to the opinion of those who hold that the relative pronoun is omitted together with part of its clause, meaning: We relate a narrative mingled with truth, or We relate it while being mingled with it, or We relate their news mingled with it, or their news which is mingled with it. As for their news, as Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar mentioned, the people of the Gospel had become corrupt, their sins had grown great, their kings had transgressed, so they worshipped idols and sacrificed to the tyrants. Among those who went to great lengths in this and became exceedingly arrogant was Decius (Diqyanus), for he exceeded all bounds in it, roamed through the lands and cities spreading corruption and mischief, and killed whoever opposed him among those who adhered to the religion of the Messiah, peace be upon him. He would pursue people and give them the choice between being killed and worshipping idols; whoever desired the lowly life of this world would do as he did, and whoever preferred the eternal life over it, he would kill, cut off his limbs, and hang them on the walls and gates of the city. When the youths, who were among the great men of their city, and it is said they were among the king's close companions, saw this, they stood up, humbled themselves before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and occupied themselves with prayer and supplication. While they were in this state, the tyrant's agents entered upon them, brought them before him, he said to them what he said, and gave them the choice between being killed and worshipping idols. They said: "Indeed we have a God who has filled the heavens and the earth with His greatness and majesty; we will never call upon any deity besides Him, and we will never acquiesce to what you call us to, ever. So decide whatever you will decide." He then ordered that the fine garments upon them be stripped off, and expelled them from his presence. He himself went out to the city of Nineveh for some matter, and gave them a respite until his return so that they might reconsider their affair; if they followed him, well and good, otherwise they would be treated as he had treated all the other believers. The youths resolved to flee with their religion and to take refuge in the sturdy cave. Each of them took something from his father's house; they gave some of it in charity and took provisions with the rest, then they went to the cave, where they began to pray in it during the hours of the night and the ends of the day, and to beseech Allah, Glorified is He, with moaning and crying out. They entrusted the matter of their sustenance to Yamlikha. Each morning he would take off his fine garments, dress in the clothes of the poor, enter the city, buy what they needed, gather news of what was happening there, and return to his companions. They continued in this state until the tyrant came to the city and sought them out, and summoned their fathers. The fathers excused themselves by saying that they had disobeyed them, plundered their wealth, scattered it in the markets, and fled to the mountain. When Yamlikha saw the evil that had befallen them, he returned to his companions weeping, with a little provision with him, and informed them of the terror he had witnessed. They turned in fear to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, fell down before Him in prostration, then raised their heads and sat conversing about their affair. While they were thus, Allah, Exalted is He, sealed their ears, so they slept with their provisions beside their heads. Decius went out in pursuit of them with his horsemen and foot soldiers, and found that they had entered the cave. He ordered them to be brought out, but no one could bring himself to enter it. When he was exhausted by them, one of them said: "Would you not have killed them had you been able to overpower them?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then build up the entrance of the cave over them, and leave them to die of hunger and thirst, and let their cave be their grave." So he did. Then there happened to them what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, related of them. ﴿Indeed they were youths﴾: this is a resumptive sentence of confirmation, implying a question from the addressee; fityah is the plural of paucity of fata, like sibyah for sabi.

﴿They believed in their Lord﴾: the shift (iltifat) was preferred to indicate that the attribute of lordship is the cause of their belief, and to take into account the statement that issued from them, as will be related of them.

﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾: by making them firm upon the religion they were following, and by manifesting to them the hidden excellences of it. In this there is a shift from the third person (absence) to the first person (speech), which is the style of the composition both in its preceding context and its flow.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 14:

﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾ That is: We made them firm, until they plunged into the narrow straits of patience in forsaking family, homeland, comfort and companions, and became bold in proclaiming the truth openly without fear or apprehension, and in refuting Decianus the tyrant.

﴿When they stood up﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "We strengthened" (rabatna). What is meant by their standing is their rising up to display the symbol of the religion. Mujahid said: They went out from the city and gathered without prior appointment. Then the eldest of them said: "Indeed I find in myself something: that my Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." They said: "We too are likewise." So they all stood up together, and ﴿they said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾. They included in their claim that which confirms its meaning and necessitates its implication, for His Lordship, glorified and exalted is He, over the two (heavens and earth) necessitates His Lordship over what is in them, that is, by way of implication. It has also been said: What is meant is their standing before the tyrant without concern for him, when he rebuked them for abandoning the worship of idols; in that case, what follows in His words, exalted is He, ﴿these...﴾ etc. is disconnected from what precedes it, being spoken by them after they left his presence. ﴿We shall never call upon﴾ we shall never worship ﴿besides Him any god﴾, another object of worship, neither independently nor as a partner. The turning away from saying "lord" (rabb) to "god" (ilah) is to specify the refutation of the opponents, since they used to call their idols gods, and to indicate that the basis of worship is the attribute of divinity, and to signal that the Lordship of Him, exalted is He, is by way of divinity and not by way of metaphorical ownership.

﴿Indeed we would have uttered an outrageous thing (shatat)﴾ That is: a statement involving shatat, that is, transgression of the limit; or a statement that is itself shatat, with the term described by the verbal noun for emphasis; then it was restricted to the descriptive form, for emphasis upon emphasis. Since worship necessarily entails speech, inasmuch as it does not lack acknowledgment of the divinity of the worshipped and supplication to Him, it was said: "Indeed we have uttered." "Idhan" (then) is a response and a conditional: that is, if we were to call upon another god besides Him, we would indeed have uttered a statement outside the bounds of reason, excessively wrongful.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 15:

﴿These⁠﴾ is the mubtada' (subject of the nominal sentence). In the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) there is a belittling of them.

﴿our people﴾ is a 'atf bayan (explicative apposition) to it.

﴿have taken besides Him gods﴾ is its khabar (predicate), and in it is the meaning of denunciation (inkar).

﴿Why do they not bring﴾ is a tahdid (urging, reproach) that carries the meaning of denunciation (inkar) and challenge (ta'jiz), i.e., "Why do they not bring ﴿against them﴾ (against their divinity, or against the soundness of their taking them as gods) ﴿a clear authority﴾ (a proof whose indication of their claim is manifestly evident)?" This is a rebuke to them and a silencing of them (iqlam hajar).

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates against Allah a lie﴾ by ascribing a partner to Him, exalted is He far above that with a great exaltation. The meaning is that he is more unjust than every wrongdoer, although the composition of the construction is on denying that he is more unjust, without addressing the denial of equality, as its verification has passed in surah Hud.

(p-211) ﴿And when you withdraw from them﴾, that is, you part from them in belief, or you intend a physical withdrawal.

﴿and what they worship other than God﴾ is coordinated with the pronoun in the accusative position (in "withdrawn from them"). "Mā" may be a relative pronoun (meaning "what") or a verbal-noun particle (mașdariyyah, meaning "the worship"). That is, "when you withdraw from them and from what they worship other than God," or "and their worship other than the worship of God." Under both readings, the exception (istithnā') is connected (muttaṣil) if they were polytheists like the people of Mecca, and disconnected (munqaṭi') if they were purely devoted to worshipping idols. It is also permissible for "mā" to be a negation, in which case it is a statement from God, Exalted, about the youths regarding monotheism, interposed between "idh" (when) and its response.

﴿then take refuge﴾, that is, seek shelter.

﴿in the cave﴾. Al-Farrā' said: it is the response to "idh," as when you say, "When you have done such-and-such, then do such-and-such." It was said: it is an indication of its response, that is, "When you withdraw from them with a withdrawal in belief, then withdraw from them with a physical withdrawal," or "If you intend to part from them, then do that by taking refuge in the cave."

﴿your Lord will spread for you﴾, that is, will extend for you and widen for you.

﴿of His mercy﴾ — ﴿your Lord﴾, the Owner of your affair, ﴿of His mercy﴾ in both abodes (this world and the Hereafter), ﴿and will prepare for you﴾, that is, will make easy for you, ﴿in your affair﴾, which you are about to undertake, namely fleeing with your religion, ﴿a means of relief﴾, that is, something by which you find comfort and benefit. It was also read with a fatḥah on the mīm and a kasrah on the fā' as a verbal noun, like "marji'" (return). The placement of "for you" (lakum) in both positions is, as has been mentioned many times, to signal from the outset that what is deferred is among their benefits, and to create anticipation for its arrival.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 17:

﴿And you see the sun﴾ is an explanation of their state after they had taken refuge in the cave. It is not stated explicitly, signalling that there is no need for it, since their conduct in accordance with the requirement of the command (to seek refuge) is evident, because it issued from sound judgment; and it relies on what preceded in His words, glorified is He: ﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave﴾, and what followed concerning the attribution of the cave to them and their being in a spacious part of it. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. It is not intended to inform of the actual occurrence of the seeing as a certainty, but rather to report that the cave was such that, were you to see it, you would see the sun.

﴿When it rises, it inclines﴾: i.e., it inclines (tatazawaru, originally tatazawaru), and it turns away, with one of the two tā' elided. It has also been read with the tā' assimilated into the zāy. It may also be tazawwaru like takhammaru, tazwārru like takhmārru, and tazwa'ir, all of which derive from al-zawr, which means inclining.

﴿away from their cave﴾ in which they took refuge; the attribution is for the slightest connection.

﴿to the right﴾: i.e., toward the right side of the cave for one who enters and heads to its depths, that is, its side which faces the west, so that its rays do not fall upon them and harm them.

﴿And when it sets﴾: i.e., you see it at its setting.

﴿it passes them by on the left﴾: i.e., it cuts them off from contact (al-qat'i'a wa al-sarm) and does not come near them.

﴿to the left﴾: i.e., toward the left side of the cave, that is, its side which faces the east. This was by God's disposing, glorified is He, in a manner that breaks habit, as an honour for them. His words, exalted is He: ﴿while they were in a spacious part of it﴾ form a circumstantial clause explaining that this is a wondrous matter, i.e., you see it inclining away from them to the right and to the left, and not circling around them, even though they were in a wide part of the cave exposed to its striking them, were it not that the hand of decree turned it away from them.

﴿That﴾: i.e., what God did for them of the sun's inclining and cutting them off at its rising and setting, while they were in the place of its rays.

﴿is among the signs of God﴾: the wondrous signs indicating the perfection of His knowledge and power, the truth of monotheism, and the honour of its adherents with Him, glorified and exalted is He. This was before Decius sealed the mouth of the cave. It has been said that the door of the cave faced north, toward the Great Bear (banat na'sh), and that the nearest risings and settings to its alignment are the point of the rising and setting of Cancer; when the sun's orbit is its orbit, it rises inclining away from it, facing its right side, which is the one nearest the west, and sets aligned with its left side, so its rays fall upon its two sides, dissolve its foulness, and temper its air, without falling upon them so as to harm their bodies and wear out their garments. Perhaps the inclination of the door toward the west was greater, and for this reason the inclining was attributed to the cave and the cutting-off to themselves. Then "that" is a reference to their taking refuge in a cave of this description. As for making it a reference to God's preservation of them in that cave for that long period, or to God's informing His Messenger (ﷺ) of their news, the context of the story does not support this reading.

﴿Whomever God guides﴾ to the truth by granting him success in it.

﴿he is the one guided﴾: the one who has attained success. The intention is either praise of them and testimony to them that they attained what they sought, and the report of the realisation of what they hoped for of the spreading of mercy and the provision of their needs; or a reminder that similar signs are many, but the one who benefits from them is the one whom God, exalted is He, has enabled to perceive them clearly.

﴿And whomever He leads astray﴾: i.e., He creates misguidance in him, turning his choice toward it.

﴿you will never find for him﴾: ever, even if you search and investigate thoroughly.

﴿any protector﴾: a helper.

﴿guide﴾: one who guides him to what has been mentioned of success, because its existence in him is impossible, not that you would fail to find him while he exists or is possible.

**[Qur'an 18:18] "And you would think them awake"**: read with a fatḥah on the sīn (*taḥsabuhum*), though it is also read with a kasrah. The address in it is as previously mentioned.

**"Ayqāẓan"** (awake) is the plural of *yaqiẓ*, which may be read with a kasrah or a fatḥah on the qāf. It means *yaqẓān* (awake). The basis of the supposition (*ḥusbān*) is that their eyes were open in the manner of one who looks. It is also said that it is because of their frequent turning. The words of God Most High, "And We turn them," do not fit this view.

**"Wa hum ruqūd"** (while they were asleep): that is, *niyām* (sleeping). This is an affirmation of what was not mentioned in what preceded, relying on its earlier mention of striking upon their ears.

**"Wa nuqallibuhum"** (And We turn them) during their sleep. **"Dhāt al-yamīn"** (to the right) is in the accusative as an adverb of place (*ẓarfiyya*), meaning the side that is adjacent to their right sides.

**"Wa dhāt al-shimāl"** (and to the left): that is, the side adjacent to their left sides, lest the earth consume the parts of their bodies that lie against it. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Had they not been turned, the earth would have consumed them." It is said that they were turned twice a year. It is also said that they were turned once, on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ. And it is said that it was every nine years.

It is read *yuqallibuhum* (He turns them), attributing the action to the Divine Name (ḍamīr al-jalāla), and *wa taqallubahum* (and their turning), as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that it indicates, so that the sense is: "and you see their turning."

**"Wa kalbuhum"** (and their dog): it is said that it was a dog that passed by them, followed them, and when they drove it away repeatedly it did not return. So God Most High made it speak, and it said: "Do not fear me, for I love the beloved of God Most High. So sleep, and I will guard you." It is also said that it was a shepherd's dog that followed them in their religion. This is supported by the reading *kālibuhum* (their dog), since the apparent sense is that it joined them. It is also said that it was the hunting dog of one of them, or of his field, or of his flock. Its colour is disputed: it is said that it was reddish-black (*anmar*), and it is said yellow (*aṣfar*), and it is said tawny (*aṣhab*), and other views exist. It is said that its name was Qiṭmīr; it is said Rayyān; it is said Tatūh; it is said Qiṭmūr; and it is said Thawr. Khālid ibn Maʿdān said: "There is no animal in Paradise except the dog of the People of the Cave and the donkey of Balʿam." It is also said that it was not of the species of dogs but was a lion.

**"Bāsiṭun dhirāʿayhi"** (stretching out his forelegs): this is a narration of a past state, and for this reason the active participle is made to govern its object. According to al-Kisāʾī, Hishām, and Abū Jaʿfar among the Basrans, it is permissible for it to govern in all cases. The *dhirāʿ* (forearm) is from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.

**"Bil-waṣīd"** (at the threshold): that is, at the place of the entrance of the cave. **"Law iṭṭalaʿta ʿalayhim"** (if you had looked upon them): that is, if you had observed them and seen them. The basic meaning of *ittilāʿ* is to overlook something by direct sight and observation. It is also read with a ḍammah on the wāw.

**"La-wallayta minhum firāran"** (you would have turned away from them in flight): fleeing from what you witnessed of them. It is either in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in sense from what precedes it, since "turning away" and "fleeing" come from one valley; or in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), by making the verbal noun carry the sense of the active participle, meaning "fleeing"; or by making the agent a verbal noun for emphasis (mubālagha), as in the saying: "it is only advance and retreat"; or it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu).

**"Wa lamuli'ta minhum ruʿban"** (and you would have been filled with terror of them): it is also read with a ḍammah on the ʿayn, meaning a fear that fills the breast and terrifies it. It is either a second object or a specifying accusative (tamyīz). This is because of the awe and the appearance with which God, Mighty and Majestic, had clothed them. Their eyes were open like one who is awake and about to speak. It is also said that it was because of the length of their nails and their hair. But this is not supported by their words: "We have remained a day or part of a day" [18:19], and His words: "and let him not make anyone aware of you" [18:19], for the apparent meaning of these is that their states did not differ in themselves. It is also said that it was because of the greatness of their bodies. Perhaps the placement of this after the mention of turning away is to indicate that each of the two is independently consequent upon the looking, for if the order of existence had been observed, the sense of the whole would have immediately suggested that it is consequent upon the whole as such. It also indicates that the terror does not cease with flight, as is customary.

It is reported from Muʿāwiya: when the Romans invaded and he passed by the cave, he said: "Uncover these for us so that we may look at them." Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said to him: "That is not for you. God Most High has prevented one better than you when He said: 'If you had looked upon them'... the verse." Muʿāwiya said: "I will not desist until I know their condition." So he sent some men and said to them: "Go and look." They did so, and when they entered the cave, God Most High sent a wind that burned them.

It is read *lallayta* with a shaddah on the lām, for intensification, and with the hamza replaced by a yāʾ, both with and without the shaddah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 19:

﴿And thus We raised them up﴾ i.e., just as We put them to sleep, and preserved their bodies from decay and dissolution, as a sign indicating the perfection of Our power, We raised them from sleep.

﴿That they might question one another﴾ i.e., that some of them might ask others, so that there would follow from it what has been explained of the profound wisdoms. Making it the purpose (ghayah) of the raising, whereas the raising was previously explained by the test (ikhtibar), is because it is among its rulings that follow from it. Limiting the mention to it is because it entails all its other effects.

﴿Said﴾ is a resumptive (isti'naf, a new sentence) to explain their questioning.

﴿One of them, a speaker﴾ was their leader, and his name was Maksilmina.

﴿How long have you remained﴾ in your sleep? He perhaps said this because he saw that their state contravened what is customary in general.

﴿They said﴾ i.e., some of them.

﴿We have remained a day or part of a day.﴾ It is said that they said this because they had entered the cave in the early morning, and their waking was at the end of the day, so they said: "We have remained a day." Then, when they saw that the sun had not yet set, they said: "Or part of a day." This was based on the prevailing assumption, so they were not attributed to lying.

﴿They said﴾ i.e., another group among them, by what occurred to them of the proofs, or by inspiration from God, glorified is He.

﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained.﴾ i.e., you do not know the duration of your remaining, and only God, glorified is He, knows it. This is a reply from them to the first group in the most courteous manner of observing good manners, and by it the division into the two well-known parties previously mentioned is realized. It has been said that all the speakers were of both parties, but in two states; the noble composition does not support this, for the resumption (isti'naf) in the narration and the address in the narrated speech require that the speech proceed upon the manner of dialogue (muhawarah) and reply (mujawabah). Otherwise it would have been said: "Then they said: Our Lord knows best how long we have remained."

﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city﴾ They said this turning away from delving deeply into the inquiry, and attending to what concerns them according to the circumstance, as the "fa'" (so) indicates. "Al-Warq" is silver, minted or unminted. Describing it with the demonstrative indicates that the speaker handed it to one of his companions so that he might buy with it their food for that day. It was read with a sukun on the ra' and idgham of the qaf into the kaf, and with a kasra on the waw and a sukun on the ra' with idgham. Their carrying it is evidence that seeking provision does not contradict reliance upon God, exalted is He.

﴿Then let him look to see which is the purest in food﴾ i.e., its people.

﴿purest﴾ most lawful and best, or most abundant and cheapest.

﴿food, and let him bring you provision from it﴾ i.e., from that purest food.

﴿And let him be gentle﴾ let him take care to be gentle in dealing, lest he be cheated, or in concealment, lest he be recognized.

﴿And let him not make anyone aware of you﴾ among the people of the city, for that would invite the spread of news about you. That is, let him not do anything that leads to that. Thus the prohibition on the first reading is establishing (ta'sis), and on the second reading it is emphasis (ta'kid) of the command to be gentle.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 20:

﴿Indeed they﴾ is a causal explanation of what preceded of the command and prohibition, meaning: let him be thorough in gentleness and in not drawing attention; because they, ﴿if they come upon you﴾, that is, they discover you, or they overpower you. The pronoun refers to the "people" (ahl) implied in "ayyuha" (the one).

﴿they would stone you﴾, if you remain upon what you are upon.

﴿or return you to their religion (milla)﴾, that is, make you revert to it and enter you into it by compulsion. It is from "al-'awd" (return) in the sense of becoming, like His exalted saying: ﴿or you will certainly return to our religion﴾. And it was said: they were originally upon their religion. The choice of the word "fi" (in) over "ila" (to) is to indicate permanence, which is the most hateful thing to them. And the mention of the possibility of stoning before the possibility of return is because the apparent state of them is steadfastness upon the religion that leads to it. The pronoun of address in the four places is for the sake of emphasis regarding the one being sent, concerning concealment, and to urge the rest to attention to the recommendation, for sincere counsel is more readily accepted, and a person's concern for his own affair is greater and more complete.

﴿And you would never succeed then﴾, that is, if you enter it, even under compulsion and coercion, you will never gain any good.

﴿ever﴾, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. And in it is a degree of severity in the warning that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 21:

﴿And thus﴾ meaning: just as We put them to sleep and raised them up, for what has passed regarding their increase in the stations of certainty.

﴿We caused [people] to come upon them﴾ meaning: We made the people aware of them, ﴿so that they might know﴾ meaning: those whom We caused to come upon them, through what they witnessed of their wondrous conditions,

﴿that the promise of God﴾ meaning: His promise of resurrection, or what He promised, which is the resurrection, or that all His promise, or all that He promised, is [true], so that His promise of resurrection, or the promised resurrection, is included in it in the first instance.

﴿is true﴾ truthful, with no falsehood in it, or established, with no turning back from it, because their sleep and their waking were like the state of one who dies and is then raised.

﴿and that the Hour﴾ meaning: the Resurrection, which is an expression for the time when all creatures are raised for reckoning and recompense,

﴿there is no doubt about it﴾ there is no doubt about its coming. For whoever witnesses that He, exalted and high, took their souls and held them for three hundred years and more, preserving their bodies from dissolving and crumbling, and then returned them to them, will have no trace of doubt that the promise of God, exalted is He, is true, and that He raises those in the graves, returning their spirits to them, and then reckons with them and recompenses them according to their deeds.

﴿when they disputed﴾ this is a temporal clause governed by His saying "We caused [them] to come upon," and its object has been placed before it to show the full concern with mentioning it, not governed by His saying "so that they might know," as has been said, because that would imply that the dispute arose after the discovery, which is not the case. The meaning is: We caused them to come upon them at the time when they were disputing

﴿among themselves about their affair﴾ so that the disagreement would be removed and the truth made clear. It has been said: the matter in dispute was the affair of their religion, since they differed about the resurrection: some affirmed it, some denied it, one said it was the resurrection of spirits without bodies, and another said it was the resurrection of both together. It has been said: the king of the city at that time was a righteous, believing man, and the people of his realm had differed about the resurrection in the manner described. So the king entered his house, closed its door, put on a hair shirt, sat on ashes, and asked his Lord to make the truth manifest. Then God, mighty and majestic, put into the heart of a man among their shepherds [the idea] to demolish what Diqyanus (Decius) had used to block the door of the cave, so that he might make it an enclosure for his sheep. At that point God raised them up, and what passed between them of talk passed. It is related that when the one who was raised entered the city, he took out a dirham to buy food with it, and it bore the stamp of Diqyanus. They accused him of having found a treasure, so they took him to the king, and he related the story to him. Some of them said: "Our fathers told us that some youths fled with their religion from Diqyanus, so perhaps these are they." The king and the people of the city, Muslim and unbeliever alike, set out and saw them and spoke with them. Then the youths said to the king: "We entrust you to God, and we seek refuge with Him for you from the evil of mankind and jinn," and then they returned to their resting places, and died. The king threw his garments over them and made for each of them a coffin of gold, but he saw them in a dream disliking gold, so he made the coffins of teak. He built a mosque over the mouth of the cave. It has also been said: when they reached the cave, the youth said to them: "Stay where you are until I enter first, lest they be frightened," so he entered and the entrance was hidden from them, so they built a mosque there. It has been said: the matter in dispute was the affair of the youths before their resurrection, meaning: We caused them to come upon them at the time when they were discussing among themselves their affair, and what passed between them and Diqyanus of conditions and terrors, and they received that from legends and from the mouths of men. In either case, the "fa" in His saying, exalted and majestic, ﴿then they said﴾ is an elliptical (faṣīḥa) "fa," meaning: We caused them to come upon them, so they saw what they saw and died, and then they said, meaning some of them said:

﴿Build over them﴾ meaning: over the entrance of their cave,

﴿a building﴾ so that people would not gain access to them, out of jealousy for their dust and to guard it. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Their Lord knows best about them﴾ is from the speech of the disputants, as if, when they saw they could not arrive at the true nature of their condition, in terms of lineage, in terms of number, and in terms of how long they remained in the cave, they said this, committing the matter to the Knower of the unseen. Or it is from the speech of God, exalted is He, in reply to the words of those who were engaged in discussing it among those disputants. It has been said: it refers to their affair and their arrangement at their death, or their condition in death and sleep, where they differed as to whether they had died or slept, as in the first instance. So "when" here is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said﴾, and they are the king and the Muslims.

﴿We will surely take over them a mosque﴾. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they said﴾ is coordinated with ﴿they disputed﴾. The choice of the past tense form indicates that this saying is not of the kind that continues and renews itself, like the disputing. It has been said: it is connected to an implied "remember." As for its connection to "We caused [them] to come upon," that is impossible, because their discovery did not take place during the time of their disputing about what is mentioned, but before it. Making the time of the disputing extended, such that the discovery occurs within part of it and the disputing within another part, is an artificial forcing that is not hidden, especially since there is no specifier for its being attached to the disputing, which comes later in occurrence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 22:

﴿They will say﴾ The pronoun in the three verbs refers to those who disputed about their story in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), from among the People of the Book and the Muslims, but not in the sense that each of them is attributed to all of them, rather to some of them. ﴿Three, the fourth of them is their dog﴾ That is: they are three persons, the fourth of them, i.e., making them four by his joining them. "Their dog": it is said that the Jews said it. It is also said that al-Sayyid of the Christians of Najran said it, and he was a Jacobite. And it was read: (Thalla'ah), with the assimilation of the thaa into the taa.

﴿And they will say: five, the sixth of them is their dog﴾ It is said that the Christians said it, or al-'Aqib among them, and he was a Nestorian.

﴿Guessing at the unseen﴾ Casting at a hidden matter whose knowledge no one has, or a conjecture about the unseen, from their saying "rajama bi-al-zann" when he conjectured. Its accusative is in the circumstantial (hal) position from the pronoun in both verbs together, that is: "casting". Or it is in the verbal-noun (masdar) position of both of them, for the casting and the saying are one. Or it is from an omitted, resumptive (mustanaf) element standing in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of both verbs together, that is: they cast a cast. The omission of the sin (for future tense) is for the sufficiency of its being conjoined to what has that.

﴿And they will say: seven, and the eighth of them is their dog﴾ This is what the Muslims say by way of receiving it from this revelation, and what is in it that guides them to that, from not placing it in the string of "casting at the unseen," and changing its composition by adding the waw that indicates the increase of the firmness of the attribution between its two parts, not by another revelation as it is said. ﴿Say﴾ affirming the truth and refuting the first ones: ﴿My Lord knows best﴾ that is: more powerful in knowledge ﴿of their number﴾ of their count ﴿none knows them﴾ that is: none knows their number, or none knows them, let alone knows their number.

﴿Except a few﴾ of the people, whom God Most High has granted success to cite those evidences. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said: when the waw occurred, the count was cut off, and upon this rests the saying of his, may God be pleased with him: "I am of that few." And if there were another revelation about that, it would not have been hidden from him, nor would he have needed to cite the waw, and the Muslims would have been his equals in knowledge of that. And from 'Ali, may God honor his face, that they were seven men whose names were Bamlikha, Maksalmina and Mashlimina, these were the companions of the king's right; and on his left were Marnush, Dabarnu and Shadhnush, and he used to consult these six in his affair; and the seventh was the shepherd who agreed with them when they fled from their king Diqyanus, and his name was Kafyashtatyush.

﴿So do not dispute﴾ The fa' is for the consequence of the prohibition upon what came before it, that is: since you have known the ignorance of the people of the first two sayings, do not argue with them.

﴿Concerning them﴾ regarding the matter of the youths ﴿except with an apparent dispute﴾ to the extent that the revelation has touched upon their description by casting at the unseen, and the absence of knowledge in a general manner, and entrusting knowledge to God, glorified be He, without explicitly declaring their ignorance and exposing them, for that would impair the noble morals.

﴿And do not seek a ruling concerning them﴾ regarding their affair ﴿from any of them﴾ from among the disputants ﴿anyone﴾ for in what has been related to you there is sufficiency from that, together with the fact that they have no knowledge of that. 'Ata' said: "except a few of the People of the Book," so the three pronouns in the three verbs are for them, and what has been mentioned of the evidences is for guiding the believers to the correctness of the third saying. In it there is an escape from what is in the first of artificiality in making one of the related sayings, arranged in a single string, a product of the narration, while the last two are otherwise; and clarity regarding the reason for omitting the object in "do not dispute." The meaning then: since you have come to know that they are not all in error in that, do not dispute with them except with a dispute that is manifest, spoken by the clear revelation, without declaring all of them ignorant, for among them there is one who is correct, though few. The prohibition on seeking a ruling is to remove what might be imagined of the possibility of its permissibility, or the possibility of its occurrence based on the correctness of some of them. The meaning: do not refer to them concerning the affair of the youths, and do not accept the third saying from the standpoint of its coming from them, but from the standpoint of its being received from the revelation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 23:

﴿And never say of anything﴾ i.e., for the sake of anything that you resolve upon.

﴿"Indeed I will do that"﴾ (p-217) the thing.

﴿tomorrow﴾ i.e., in future time absolutely, so that "tomorrow" enters into it as its primary (meaning) instance. For it was revealed when the Jews said to the Quraysh: "Ask him about the spirit, about the People of the Cave, and about Dhu al-Qarnayn." So they asked him (ﷺ), and he said: "Come to me tomorrow and I will inform you," without adding "if Allah wills" (istithna'). So the revelation was delayed for him until it distressed him, and the Quraysh denied him. As for what has been said, that the direct meaning of the expression is tomorrow, and that what follows it is understood by way of the implication of the text (dalalat al-nass), it is refuted by the fact that what comes after it does not share its meaning in the ground of the prohibition (manat al-nahy), for the breadth of scope is itself evidence of capability. So let it be pondered:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 24:**

﴿Unless Allah wills.﴾ This is an *istithna' mufarragh* (an exception whose main clause is left unstated, here the prohibition). The meaning is: do not say that in any state except the state of its being connected to Allah's will, in the usual manner, which is to say: "If Allah wills." Or [it means]: at no time except the time when Allah wills [that you say it]. Not absolutely, but rather subject to His will at that moment, for forgetting is also by His will, may He be exalted. There is no justification for attaching it to the agent, because it is not sound to make the will's conjunction with the act an exception, and because an exception that makes the will an objection to the prohibition is incompatible [with the sense]. It has also been said: the exception functions as a means of emphasis (*ta'bid*), as if it were said: "Never say it," like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for us to return to it, unless Allah wills﴾ (7:89).

﴿And remember your Lord﴾ by your saying "If Allah wills," seeking to overtake [your lapse] by it.

﴿When you forget﴾: when some forgetting has come from you, and then you remember it. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "Even after a year, so long as one has not broken the oath." For this reason, delaying the exception has been permitted. But the majority of jurists hold otherwise, since if that were valid, no acknowledgment (*iqrar*), no divorce (*talaq*), and no manumission (*ataq*) would be established, and truthfulness or falsehood could not be known. Al-Qurtubi said: this applies to making up for blessing (*tabarruk*) and escaping sin. As for an exception that changes the ruling, it can only be connected [immediately]. It is also possible that the meaning is: "Remember your Lord with glorification and seeking forgiveness when you forget the exception," as an intensification of urging toward it; or: "Remember your Lord and His punishment when you have abandoned some of what He commanded you, so that this may move you to make up for it"; or: "Remember Him when forgetfulness overtakes you, so that He may remind you of what was forgotten." It has been understood as referring to performing a forgotten prayer when one remembers it.

﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me﴾: that is, will grant me success.

﴿to something nearer than this﴾: that is, to something nearer and clearer than the story of the People of the Cave among the signs and proofs that indicate my prophethood.

﴿to a right course (rashadan)﴾: that is, guidance for people and a sign pointing to it. Indeed, He, may He be mighty and majestic, did so, for He gave him clear proofs greater and more evident than that, such as the stories of the prophets whose days are far apart, and the events that will occur in future ages until the Hour. Or [it means]: "to one nearer in right guidance and closer in report than what was forgotten."

ۚ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾ — this is a resumed sentence (جملة مستأنفة) explaining what was left general in what preceded, and it points to the difficulty of attaining its knowledge. It is also said that it is a report of the speech of the People of the Book, for they differed concerning the length of their stay just as they differed concerning their number: some of them said "like this," and some said three hundred. It is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The People of the Book hold that they remained three hundred solar years, while Allah the Exalted mentioned the lunar year, and the difference between the two in every hundred years is three years, so it comes to three hundred and nine years." "Years" (سنين) is either an explanatory apposition (عطف بيان) to "three hundred," or, it is said, a substitute (بدل). It was also read with the genitive construction (على الإضافة), placing the plural in the position of the singular; and what makes this preferable here is that the plural marker in it compensates for what was omitted in the singular, and that the original form for numbers is to be followed by a plural noun.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 26:

﴿Say: "Allah knows best how long they stayed."﴾ That is: as to the time during which they stayed there. ﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is: what is hidden within them and concealed of the conditions of their inhabitants.
