The "lam" (lam al-ikhtisas, the particle of exclusivity) here denotes exclusive knowledge (al-ikhtisas al-ilmi), not exclusive creative power (al-ikhtisas al-takwini), for He is not exclusively related to the unseen in that respect.

﴿See Him well and hear Him well.﴾ By the form of exclamation (sighat al-ta'ajjub), it indicates that the manner of His knowledge, glorified is He, of things seen and things heard, lies beyond what the perception of perceivers comprehends. Nothing veils it, nothing stands between it and its object, and with respect to Him the subtle and the dense, the small and the great, the hidden and the manifest do not differ. The pronoun "hu" refers to the Divine Name (Allah), and its position is in the nominative as the agent. The "ba'" (bi-) is superfluous according to Sibawayh. Its original form was "abṣar", meaning "he became one who has sight"; then it was transferred to the imperative form for the sake of creating the command, so the pronoun appeared explicitly because the imperative form is not suitable for it, or because of the superfluous "ba'", as in "kafā bihi" (sufficient is He). The accusative is as the object according to al-Akhfash. The agent is the pronoun of the one addressed, who is every person; and the "ba'" is superfluous if the hamzah is for transitivity (ta'diyah), and transitive if the hamzah is for becoming (sayrurah). Perhaps the mention of the matter of His seeing, exalted is He, is first because what we are concerned with is of the category of things seen.

﴿They have no protector⁠⁠ besides Him﴾ — for the people of the heavens and the earth — ﴿besides Him﴾, exalted is He.

﴿Of any guardian⁠⁠﴾ who manages their affairs and helps them independently.

﴿And He does not make anyone a partner in His command﴾ — in His judgment, or in the knowledge of the unseen.

﴿Anyone﴾ among them, and no share in it is granted to them. And this, as you see, is more emphatic in negating a partner than saying: "no guardian and no partner." It was also read in the imperative form of the prohibition addressed to a present person, with the address being to every individual. Since the arrangement of the noble Qur'an indicates the story of the People of the Cave, from the standpoint that it is, with respect to the Prophet ﷺ, among the matters of the unseen, and as a miraculous revelation, He commanded the Prophet ﷺ to be constant in studying it, so He said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 27:

﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾ and do not listen to their saying, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it."

﴿There is none who can alter His words﴾ no one other than Him is able to alter or change them.

﴿And you will not find﴾ ever, no matter how much you seek.

﴿Any refuge besides Him﴾ a refuge to which one turns when a calamity befalls.

﴿And restrain yourself﴾: hold it back, and keep it steadfast in companionship.

﴿with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾: meaning, constantly devoted to supplication at all times. It was also said: at some part of the day. It is read as (بِالغُدْوَةِ) (bil-ghudwah), with the definite article attached to it, although it is usually a proper noun, on the interpretation that it is indefinite in meaning because of them. By "them" is meant the poor among the believers, such as Ṣuhayb, ʿAmmār, Khabbāb, and others, may Allah be pleased with them. It was also said that they were the Ahl al-Ṣuffa (the poor Companions who lived in a shaded area of the Prophet's mosque), who numbered about seven hundred men. It is said that some leaders of the disbelievers said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Remove these mawālī (freedmen and lowly clients), whose smell is like the smell of sheep, so that we may sit with you," just as the people of Noah, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Shall we believe in you when the lowest people follow you?﴾ So this was revealed. The expression of them by the relative clause serves to give the reason for the command, through what is contained in the scope of the relative clause, namely the quality that calls for continuing the companionship. ﴿desiring﴾ by their supplication ﴿His Face﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the concealed pronoun in (يَدْعُونَ), meaning: seeking His good pleasure, may He be exalted, and obedience to Him.

﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾: meaning, let your gaze not go beyond them to others. Its use with (عَنْ) is either because it is made to imply the meaning of turning away, or it means: do not turn your eyes away from them toward others, from ʿadawtuhu ʿan al-amr, meaning I turned him away from the matter, the object being omitted because it is evident. It is also read as (وَلا تُعْدِ عَيْنَيْكَ) and (وَلا تُعَدِّ عَيْنَيْكَ), from the causative and transitive forms, and the intent is the prohibition to him, ﷺ, against looking down upon them because of the shabbiness of their attire, while aspiring to the attire of the rich.

﴿desiring the adornment of the life of this world﴾: meaning, seeking the company of the nobles, the rich, and the people of worldly wealth. It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the (ka) pronoun according to the first reading of the well-known recitation, and from the subject according to the second reading of it. The pronoun in (تُرِيدُ) refers to the two eyes, and attributing the desire to them is metaphorical; its being singular is because of the mutual connection, as in his saying:

*For whom is a slippery slope, on which both eyes slip and pour forth.*

It is also from the concealed pronoun in the verb according to the last two readings.

﴿And do not obey﴾ in removing the poor from your gatherings.

﴿whose heart We have made heedless﴾: meaning, We made it heedless, because its readiness for remembrance has been entirely nullified; or We found it heedless, like your saying: "I found him a coward" and "I found him a miser," when you find him as such; or it is from aghfala ibilahu, meaning, We did not mark him with remembrance.

﴿of Our remembrance﴾: like those who ask you to drive the poor away from your gathering. Indeed they are heedless of Our remembrance, contrary to what the believers do of supplication at the gatherings of times. In this there is an indication that what drives them to this rejection is the heedlessness of their hearts from the presence of Allah, may He be glorified, and from His direction, and their immersion in sensible things, until it became hidden from them that nobility lies in the adornment of the soul, not in the adornment of the body. It is also read as (أغْفَلَنا قَلْبُهُ), with the verb attributed to the heart, meaning: it considered us heedless of His remembrance of it with punishment, from aghfaltuhu, when you find him heedless.

﴿and followed his desire, and his affair was neglect﴾: meaning, loss and ruin; or one who precedes the truth and the right, casting it behind his back, from their saying: "a fursun (horse) furus," meaning one that precedes the horses. Or it means excess and neglect, for heedlessness of His remembrance, may He be glorified, leads to following desire, which leads to transgression and distance from truth and right. The expression of them by the relative clause serves to signal the causal force of what is contained in the scope of the relative clause for the prohibition against obeying them.

﴿And say﴾ to those heedless ones who follow their desires: ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾. That is: what has been revealed to me is the truth and nothing else, coming from your Lord. Or, the meaning is: the truth known to come from your Lord, not from me, so that it could be imagined to be altered or so that it could be possible to hesitate in following it. His Exalted saying, ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾, is either a continuation of the statement commanded to be said, and the "fa'" (fa', the particle of consequence) here indicates the ordering of what follows upon what precedes by way of threat, not as a result derived from it, as in His saying: ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold without reckoning﴾. And His saying: ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be of the doubters﴾, means: once it is established that what has been revealed to me is truth without doubt, and that this truth is from your Lord, then whoever wishes to believe in it, let him believe like the rest of the believers, and let him not offer as an excuse what can hardly serve as an excuse. And whoever wishes to disbelieve in it, let him do so. In this there is a great deal of threat, and a display of independence from following them, and indifference to them and to their belief, whether it exists or not, which is not hidden.

Or it is a threat from God Exalted, and the "fa'" indicates that what follows of threat is ordered upon the command itself, not upon the content of the commanded statement. The meaning is: say to them that, and after that, whoever wishes to believe in it, or to accept your word concerning it, let him believe; and whoever wishes to disbelieve in it, or to deny you concerning it, let him do so. Then His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared﴾ is a severe warning, an emphasis on the threat, and a justification for what it implies of restraint from disbelief, or for what is understood from the apparent choice: the indifference to their disbelief and the scant concern for restraining them from it, for preparing its recompense is among the causes of respite and delay. According to the first interpretation, it is a justification for the command with the mentioned threatening choice, that is: say to them that, since We have prepared ﴿for the wrongdoers﴾, that is, We have readied for those who disbelieve in the truth after it has come from God, Glorified is He. The expression of them as "the wrongdoers" serves to draw attention to the fact that the will to disbelieve and choosing it is transgression beyond the limit, and placing a thing in other than its place.

﴿A Fire﴾: great and marvelous.

﴿Encompasses them﴾: that is, it encompasses them. The choice of the past form indicates certainty.

﴿Its enclosure﴾: that is, its tent. What encompasses them of the fire is likened to it. It was said: the suradiq is the chamber that surrounds the tent. It was said: its suradiq is its smoke. It was said: a wall of fire.

﴿And if they ask for relief﴾: from thirst.

﴿They will be relieved with water like molten brass﴾: like molten iron. It was said: like the dregs of oil, and this is in the manner of the saying: "fa-i'tabu bi-l-saylam" (a poetic expression).

﴿It scalds the faces﴾: when it is brought near to be drunk, the face is scorched by its heat. From the Prophet (ﷺ): it is like the dregs of oil; when it is brought close to him, the skin of his face falls off.

﴿Wretched is the drink﴾: that.

﴿And evil is the resting place﴾: the Fire. ﴿A couch﴾ (murtafaqan): a place of reclining. The original meaning of "ittifaq" (reclining) is placing the elbow beneath the cheek. And how is that in the Fire? Rather, it is in contrast to His saying: ﴿and good is the resting place﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 30:

﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ is in the position of a causal clause (ta'lil) justifying the exhortation to faith that is understood from the offering of choice (takhyir). It is as if it were said: "And those who believed." Perhaps the change of its composition (sabk) is to signal the complete contrast between the outcomes of the two groups, i.e.: indeed, those who believed in the truth that was revealed to you.

﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ as has been explained in its elaborations (tada'if).

﴿Indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾. The predicate of the first "inna" is the second "inna" together with what is in its scope (hayyiz). The returning pronoun (al-raji') is omitted, i.e.: "one who does better of them in deed" (man ahsana minhum 'amalan), or it is dispensed with, as in your saying: "What a fine man Zayd is" (ni'ma al-rajulu Zaydan). Or it occupies the place of the apparent noun, for the one who truly does the better deed is the one who believed and did righteous deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 31:

﴿Those﴾, who are described by the sublime attributes, ﴿for them are gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining the reward. Alternatively, ﴿for them are gardens of Eden﴾ is the predicate, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD). Or it is a second predicate following the first.

﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾. The first "min" (mina) is inceptive (ibtida'iyya, indicating the starting point), and the second "min" is explicative (bayaniyya, specifying the kind), describing "bracelets." The indefiniteness of "bracelets" (asawir) is for magnification (tafkhim). It is the plural of "uswira" or "asawir," the plural of "siwar."

﴿And they will wear green garments﴾. Green is singled out for their garments because it is the most beautiful of colours and the most fresh and soft.

﴿Of fine green silk and brocade﴾. That is, cushions of silk brocade (dibaj) and of coarser material. Both kinds are combined to indicate that therein is what the souls desire and what delights the eyes.

﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾. On thrones, as is the custom of those who live in luxury.

﴿How excellent a reward﴾, that.

﴿And how good a resting place﴾: that is, the couches, ﴿as a resting place﴾ (p-221) that is, a place of reclining.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 32:

﴿And strike for them﴾ i.e., for the two groups, the disbelieving and the believing, ﴿a parable: two men﴾. They are two objects of "strike" (iḍrib), the first being the second, because it is the one in need of detail and explanation. That is: strike for the disbelievers and the believers a parable, not in terms of their conditions, which are understood from what was mentioned just before, namely that for the first group in the Hereafter there is such-and-such, and for the latter there is such-and-such, but rather in terms of the disobedience of the first group alongside their enjoyment of the blessings of God Most High, and the obedience of the latter alongside their bearing the hardships of poverty; for example, the condition of two men, either hypothetical or actual, who were two brothers from the Children of Israel, or two partners. The disbeliever's name was Qatrus, and the believer's name was Yahudha. They divided eight thousand dinars between them. The disbeliever used his share to buy property and land, while the believer spent his share on the avenues of righteousness. Their affair then ended in what God Most High related. It was also said: they were two brothers from the Banu Makhzum: the disbeliever was al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Asad, and the Muslim was Abu Salama 'Abdullah ibn 'Abd al-Asad, the first husband of Umm Salama (may Allah be pleased with her).

﴿We made for one of them﴾ namely the disbeliever,

﴿two gardens﴾ orchards ﴿of grapevines﴾ of varied vines. The whole clause is an explanation of the parable, or a description of the two men.

﴿And We surrounded them with palm trees﴾ i.e., We made the palm trees encircle them, with their vines enclosed by them. It is said: "ḥaffahu al-qawm" when people went around him, and "ḥafaftuhu bihim" when you made them surround him; so the preposition bi- makes it take a second object, as in your saying: "ghashshaytuhu bihi" (I covered him with it).

﴿And We placed between them﴾ in the midst of the two.

﴿cultivated land﴾ so that each of them would combine foodstuffs and fruits, continuously cultivated, in a pleasing arrangement and a graceful layout.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 33:

﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce﴾ (their fruit), and it reached a suitable stage for eating. It was also read with the vowel on the kaf sukun (ukulaha, pronounced with a sukun). It was also read: "Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce" (kull al-jannatayn atā ukulahu).

﴿And did not fall short in it at all﴾ (lam tanqus min ukulihā), i.e., it did not diminish any of its produce.

﴿Anything﴾ (shay'an), as is customary in all orchards, for fruit is generally abundant in one year and scarce in another, and likewise some trees bear fruit in some years and not in others.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾ (between each of the two gardens) ﴿a river﴾ (nahran) of its own, so that their irrigation would endure and their splendor would increase. It was also read with the lightened form (bi-l-takhfif). Perhaps the mention of the gushing of the river is placed after the mention of the bringing forth of produce, although the external order is the reverse, in order to signal that each of the bringing forth of produce and the gushing of the river is independent in completing the excellences of the two gardens, as in the story of the cow and similar passages. Had the order been reversed, it would be understood that the whole was a single attribute, some parts of which follow from others, since the bringing forth of produce ordinarily branches from irrigation. There is also in it an indication that the bringing forth of produce does not depend on irrigation, as in His saying: ﴿Its oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 34:

﴿And he had fruit﴾: for the owner of the two gardens, there were kinds of wealth other than the two gardens, from the verb thamara (to make wealth abundant), meaning he made his wealth increase. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is all of his wealth, of gold, silver, livestock and other things. Mujahid said: it is gold and silver specifically.

﴿So he said to his companion﴾: the believer, ﴿while he was﴾, that is, the one who was speaking,

﴿debating with him﴾: that is, with his believing companion, though the reverse is also permissible; that is, he was returning to him in speech, from the verb hara (to return), ﴿"I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men"﴾: in retinue (hashm) and helpers, or in male children, because they are the ones who go forth (yanfirun) with him.

(p-222) ﴿And he entered his garden﴾, which has had its circumstances, its number, its attributes, its features, and its (singular) designation described, either because the purpose does not depend on enumerating them, or because one of them is joined to the other, or because entering happens to one after another.

﴿While he was wronging himself﴾, harming himself through his conceit and his disbelief.

﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the mention of his entering his garden while he was wronging himself, as if it were said: "What did he say at that time?" So it is answered: he said, ﴿"I do not think that this will ever perish"﴾, that is, that it will be annihilated ﴿ever﴾, because of his long hope, his persistence in heedlessness, and his being deceived by the respite granted to him. Perhaps he said this in response to the admonition of his companion, his reminder of the perishing of his two gardens, his prohibition against being deceived by them, and his command to acquire the enduring good deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 36:

﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, occurring in what is to come.

﴿And if I am returned﴾ to my Lord through resurrection at its establishment, as you say, ﴿I will surely find﴾ on that day ﴿better than this﴾, i.e., better than this garden. It is also read: (better than both of them), i.e., than the two gardens.

﴿A return (munqalaban)﴾: a place of return, and an outcome. The basis of this hope and of the false oath is the belief that He, exalted is He, bestowed what He bestowed upon him in this world only because of his inherent worthiness and his nobility before Him, glorified is He; and he did not realize that this was a gradual drawing-on (istidraj).

﴿His companion said to him﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnaf*, a new clause that continues the narrative), as mentioned before. ﴿while he was conversing with him﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah ḥāliyyah*), as mentioned before. Its purpose is to alert the reader from the outset that what follows is speech of great importance, presented for the sake of dialogue.

﴿Do you disbelieve﴾ in that you said, "I do not think the Hour will ever come."

﴿in the One who created you﴾, meaning: within the creation of your origin.

﴿from dust﴾. The creation of Adam (peace be upon him) from dust includes the creation of every human being from dust, since the creation of each individual of mankind has a share in the creation of Adam (peace be upon him). His noble nature was not confined to himself; rather, it was a pattern that comprised, in a general way, the nature of all members of the species, with its effects extending to all of them. Thus, his creation from dust was a creation of all of them from it. It has also been said that the meaning is: "He created you from it," because it is the root of your material, since through it nourishment is obtained, and from nourishment the semen is produced. So reflect on this.

﴿then from a drop [of semen]﴾: this is your nearer material. The created being is one, while the beginnings are multiple.

﴿then fashioned you into a man﴾, meaning: He made you proportionate, completed you as a male human being, or made you a man. The expression of Him, exalted is He, by the relative pronoun (*al-mawṣūl*) indicates that what occurs in the relative clause (*ṣilah*) is the reason for denying disbelief, and it alludes to the proof of resurrection, which is expressed by the words of the Mighty One, the Lord of all: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust﴾ … etc.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 38:

﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord﴾. Its original form is "lakin anna" (لَكِنْ إنّا), and it has also been recited thus. The hamza was dropped, so the two nuns came together and were assimilated (al-idgham), and the result is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n, the pronoun referring to the situation or affair). "Huwa" (هُوَ) is the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is "Allah rabbi" (اللَّهُ رَبِّي), and that whole sentence is the predicate of "inna" (إنّا), with the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) in it referring back to it. It has also been recited with the alif of "inna" retained in connected speech, in pause, and in both, and in pause specifically. It has also been recited as "lakinnahu" (لَكِنَّهُ) with a haa, and as "lakin" with "inna" omitted, and as "lakin inna la ilaha illa huwa rabbi" (لَكِنْ إنّا لا إلَهَ إلّا هو رَبِّي). The point of the contrast (al-istidrak) lies in His saying, ﴿Do you disbelieve﴾ (﴿أكَفَرْتَ﴾), as if he said: "You are a disbeliever, but I am a believer who affirms the oneness of God."

﴿And I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾. In this is an indication that his disbelief was by way of association (al-ishrak). (p-223)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 39:

﴿Why did you not, when you entered your garden, say﴾: that is, "Why did you not say, when you entered it?" The placing of the adverbial phrase before the thing being urged (the verb of urging, "why did you not say") is to indicate (inda') the necessity of saying it at the very moment of entering, without delay, and not to restrict (li-l-qasr) it.

﴿"What God willed (ma sha'a Allah)"﴾: that is, "The matter is what God willed," or "What God willed came to be," with "ma" being a relative pronoun in the nominative position; or "whatever God willed came to be," with "ma" being a conditional noun in the accusative position, and the answer (jawab) being omitted. The purpose is to urge him to acknowledge that it [the garden] and what is in it are by the will of God Most High: if He wills, He preserves it, and if He wills, He annihilates it.

﴿"There is no power except through God" (la quwwata illa bi-llah)﴾: that is, "Why did you not say that, acknowledging your inability, and that whatever you were able to achieve of its cultivation and management of its affairs is only by His assistance (ma'una) and His enabling (iqdar), Most High?" From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever sees something and is impressed by it, and says: 'What God willed, there is no power except through God,' it will not harm him."

﴿"If you see me as less than you in wealth and children"﴾: "ana" is either an emphatic for the pronoun of the speaker (ya' al-mutakallim), or a pronoun of separation (damir fasl) between the two objects of the verb of seeing. If it is taken as cognitive (ilmiyya) and "aqall" is the second of them, [it is a pronoun of separation]; and if it is taken as visual (basariyya), then "ana" is at that point merely an emphasis, and "aqall" is a circumstantial (hal). This is because the condition for it to be a pronoun of separation is that it sits between the subject and the predicate, or [in a construction] whose original form is subject and predicate. It is also read as "aqullu" in the nominative as the predicate of "ana," and the clause is then a second object of the verb of seeing, or a circumstantial. In His words "and children" there is support for those who interpret the "nafar" (group/men) as children.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 40:

﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾ This is the answer to the conditional clause, and the meaning is: "If you see me as poorer than you, then I expect from the handiwork of God, glorified is He, that He will turn around what is with me and with you of poverty and wealth, so that He grants me, for my faith, a garden better than your garden, and deprives you of His blessing for your disbelief, and ruins your garden."

﴿And He sends upon it a calculation﴾ This is a verbal noun with the meaning of "reckoning," like "al-butlan" (nullification) and "al-ghufran" (forgiveness); that is, a measure which God, exalted is He, has decreed and reckoned, and it is the judgment of its destruction. It has been said: "a punishment of reckoning," meaning the reckoning of what his hands have earned. It has also been said: "al-marami," the plural of "husbaanah," which means thunderbolts. The support of the noble text in what follows is more in favor of the first view.

﴿from the sky, so that it becomes a barren, slippery ground﴾ This is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the passive participle, for emphasis; that is, a smooth ground on which one slips, because all the buildings, trees, and plants upon it have been uprooted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 41:

﴿Or it becomes⁠﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with His, exalted is He, saying: "then it becomes" (fa-tuṣbiḥa). And according to the third possibility, it is coordinated with "yursila" (He sends). ﴿Its water sinking⁠﴾ into the ground, i.e., sunk (ghā'iran) into the earth; the verbal noun (maṣdar) is used for it as an intensification (mubālaghah). ﴿Then you will never be able﴾ ever ﴿to it⁠﴾, i.e., to the sunken water.

﴿To seek it⁠﴾, let alone to find it and bring it back.

And his fruit was encompassed (ﷺ no) — let me translate accurately.

﴿And his fruit was encompassed﴾ — that is, his wealth in its familiar form, from his two gardens and what was in them, was destroyed; and its origin is from the encompassing (إحاطة) of an enemy. It is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon something implied (muqaddar), as if it were said: "So some of what he feared of the calamity befell him, and his wealth was destroyed." It was omitted because the context of the preceding and following discourse indicates it, as in the case of the conjunction preceded by the eloquent "fa" (al-fāʾ al-faṣīḥa), ﴿so he began to turn over his two palms﴾ — back side to front — and this is a metaphor (kināya) for regret, as if it were said: "So he began to regret."

﴿for what he had spent on it﴾ — that is, on its upkeep, from his wealth. Perhaps the specification of regret with it, rather than with what has now perished of the garden, is because regret occurs only over voluntary actions, and because what he spent on its upkeep was (p-224) of that which could be preserved from the vicissitudes of time; and he had spent it on its benefits, hoping — that is, that he would enjoy them more than he enjoyed them — and he thought that the hands of destruction could not reach them. For this reason he said: "I do not think that this will ever perish." So when it became clear to him that it was subject to ruin, he regretted what he had done, based on the corrupt assumption of spending what could be saved on such a quickly vanishing thing.

﴿And it﴾ — that is, the garden — of grapevines surrounded by palm trees.

﴿was fallen﴾ — collapsed ﴿upon its trellises﴾ — that is, its supports built for the vines, because they fell before the vines themselves fell. The specific mention of its state rather than the palms and the crops is either because it was the principal part, and these two complete it, or because the mention of its destruction suffices instead of mentioning the destruction of the rest, since once it was destroyed, while it was secured by its trellises, the destruction of everything else is by a fortiori reasoning; or because the expenditure on its upkeep was greater. It was said: God sent a fire that burned it, and its water sank away.

﴿And he says﴾ — a conjunction upon "turns over," or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its pronoun, that is: while he was saying ﴿"Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord!"﴾ As if he remembered his companion's admonition, and knew that he had been afflicted because of his polytheism, so he wished that he had not been a polytheist, and then he would not have suffered what he had suffered before. It is possible that this was a repentance from polytheism and a regret for what had passed from him.

﴿And he had no company (fiʼah) who could help him﴾ — read also with the feminine-to-masculine variant (yā' taḥtāniyyah, i.e., the verb with a yā' rather than a tā').

﴿who could help him﴾ — who would be able to help him by repelling the destruction, and by turning back what has been destroyed and bringing about the like of it. The pronoun is plural in meaning (jumiʻa al-ḍamīr bi-i'tibār al-maʻnā), as in His, the Exalted and Most High, saying: ﴿they see them as twice their number﴾.

﴿apart from Allah﴾ — for He alone is the One able to do that. ﴿Nor was he﴾ in himself ﴿one who could defend himself﴾, being one who protects himself by his own strength from His vengeance, glorified is He.

﴿Hunalika﴾ (there), in that situation and in that state.

﴿Al-wilayatu lillahi al-haqq﴾ (Authority belongs to God, the True). That is: victory belongs to Him alone; none is able to achieve it. This is a confirmation of what precedes it. Or it means that He gives victory to His believing friends (awliya'uhu) against the disbelievers, just as He gave victory to the believer, his brother, by what He did to the disbeliever. This is supported by His words, exalted be He: ﴿He is best in reward and best in consequence﴾, that is, for His friends. It has also been read as (al-wilayah) with a kasra on the waw, and its meaning is dominion and sovereignty: that is, there, sovereignty belongs to Him, mighty and majestic, which cannot be overcome, and from which none can escape, or other than whom none is worshipped, like His words, exalted be He: ﴿So when they board a ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾. Thus it is an alert that his words, ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord﴾... etc., were said out of compulsion and distress at what had befallen him, in the style of His words, exalted be He: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾. It has also been said: "there" points to the Hereafter, like His words, exalted be He: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is God's, the One, the Subduer﴾. It has also been read with the raf' of al-haqq as an attribute of al-wilayah, and with its nasb as an emphasizing infinitive (masdar mu'akkad). It has also been read ('uqban) with a damma on the qaf, and ('uqba) like rujha; all of them mean: the outcome (al-'aqibah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 45:

﴿And strike for them the example of the life of this world.﴾ That is: mention to them what resembles it in its splendor, its freshness, and the swiftness of its passing, so that they do not become complacent in it, nor devote themselves wholly to it, and turn away entirely from the Hereafter. Or, explain to them its wondrous attribute, which in its strangeness is like an example.

﴿Like water⦆ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the example; that is: it is like water.

﴿which We sent down from the sky﴾ It is also permissible for it to be a second object of "idrib" (strike), with the meaning of "sayyara" (make/render).

﴿So the vegetation of the earth mingled with it﴾ it became intertwined by means of it, ﴿nabat (p-225) al-ard⦆ then it grew thick and some of it mixed with other parts because of its abundance and density. Or the water seeped into the plants until they were watered and flourished. The apparent expression would then be "fakhtalaṭa bi-nabat al-ard" (mingled with the plants of the earth), but the noble composition has preferred what it has, for the sake of emphasizing abundance, since each of the two things mingled is described by the attribute of the other.

﴿Then it became﴾ that intertwined vegetation, following its brightness and freshness, ﴿hashiman⦆ broken, shattered, crumbled.

﴿which the winds scatter⦆ disperse it. It was also read as "tudhrīhi" (from adhrā, to scatter). The winds scatter it. The thing compared to is not the water itself, but the image abstracted from the whole, namely the state of plants grown by water: becoming green and lush, then dry debris that the winds carry away, as though it had not flourished yesterday.

﴿And Allah is over all things﴾ among the things which include origination and annihilation ﴿Capable⦆ able, perfectly powerful.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 46:

﴿The wealth and the sons are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ is an explanation of the status of what they used to boast of, from the embellishments of the life of this world, as the disbelieving brother said: "I have more wealth than you, and mightier in respect of men" [18:34], following the explanation of the matter of the life of this world itself by means of the parable that has passed. The mention of wealth before sons, even though sons are more esteemed than it, as in the verse cited just above and in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We aided you with wealth and sons﴾ [17:6], and other noble verses, is due to its antiquity in what it is associated with of adornment, aid, and other things. It is also due to its generality with respect to individuals and times, for it is an adornment and an aid to every one of the fathers and the sons at every time and moment. As for sons, their adornment and their aid only pertain to those who have reached the status of fatherhood. Also, because wealth is the means of the preservation of the self, and sons of the preservation of the species; because the need for it is more pressing than the need for them; because it precedes them in existence; and because it is an adornment without them, without the converse being true, for whoever has sons without wealth is in a state of straitness and hardship. The adornment is given in the singular, although it is attributed to the two, because it is originally a verbal noun that has been applied to the object (of adornment) for emphasis, as if the two themselves were the very adornment. The meaning is: what they boast of, namely wealth and sons, is a thing with which one adorns oneself in the life of this world, and its condition is known in its swift passing and nearness to annihilation; so how about what is among its attributes, which by nature pass away before it passes away? ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾ are the deeds of goodness. It is said: they are the five prayers. It is said: "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest." It is said: everything that is intended by it the face of God, exalted is He. In every case, there enters into them, as a primary entry, the deeds of the poor among the believers who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, desiring His face. As for their goodness, it is evident. As for their enduring, it is the enduring of their rewards when everything the soul aspires to of the portions of this world perishes. ﴿Are better﴾, that is: better than what has been described in its status of wealth and sons. The expression of the enduring and goodness of those deeds in the form of attributes already settled, although it is their due that they be intended for the purpose of the statement, especially in contrast to the affirmation of perishing for what corresponds to them of wealth and sons, follows the pattern of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What is with you will be exhausted, and what is with God is enduring﴾ [16:96], to signal that their enduring is a certain matter that needs no explanation; rather, the word "enduring" is a name that is itself a descriptor. For this reason the qualified noun was not mentioned. What requires addressing is only their being better.

﴿With your Lord﴾, that is: in the Hereafter. This is an explanation of the matter in which the effects of their being better become manifest, in the manner of the attribution of adornment to the life of this world, and not to indicate their superiority over wealth and sons in it, despite all sharing in the origin, since they share nothing in being better in the Hereafter.

﴿As reward﴾, returning to their possessor.

﴿And better in hope﴾, since by them their possessor attains in the Hereafter everything he used to hope for in this world. As for what has passed of wealth and sons, their possessor has no hope that he attains. The repetition of "better" is to indicate the difference in the aspect of betterness, and for emphasis in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 47:

﴿And [remember] the Day We set the mountains in motion﴾ is in the accusative case, governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Remember the time when We uproot them from their places and set them moving through the air in their [own] forms, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass by as the clouds pass﴾." Or [the meaning is]: We set their parts in motion after We make them scattered dust. The purpose of reminding them of this is to warn the polytheists of the calamities it contains. It has also been said that it is conjoined to what precedes it, from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿with your Lord﴾, meaning: the enduring good deeds are better with Allah and on the Day of Resurrection. It has been read as (tusayyaru) in the passive form from the causative (tafil), following the customs of majesty, and as a notice that there is no need to mention the agent since it is determined. It has also been read as (tasiru) [in the active]. ﴿And you see the earth﴾, meaning: all its sides. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is capable of seeing. It has been read as (tura) in the passive form.

﴿Laid bare﴾: As for the exposure of what lies beneath the mountains, it is evident. As for what lies beyond that, the mountains used to screen it from the viewer before that, but now it has become a level plain in which you see neither crookedness nor elevation.

﴿And We gather them﴾: We assemble them at the place of standing from every direction. The use of the past form after "We set in motion" and "you see" serves to indicate the certainty of the gathering, which follows from the resurrection that the deniers deny, and upon which the matter of recompense turns. Likewise is the discussion of what is conjoined to it, negated and affirmed. It has been said that it indicates that their gathering takes place before the setting in motion and the laying bare, so that they may witness those terrors, as if it were said: "And We gathered them before that."

﴿So We leave not﴾: meaning, We do not leave ﴿of them any one﴾. It is said (ghadarahu) and (aghdarahu) when he leaves him behind. From it comes (al-ghadr), which is the abandonment of fidelity, and (al-ghadir), which is the water the torrent leaves in the low-lying ground. It has been read with the letter ya' and with the letter ta' (tu'ghdar), with the verb attributed to the pronoun of the earth, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the earth casts out what is in it and empties itself﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 48:

﴿And they will be presented before your Lord﴾. Their condition is likened to that of troops presented before a sovereign so that he may command concerning them what he commands. The shift to the third person (al-ghaybah), the construction of the verb in the passive voice together with the mention of the title of Lordship (al-rububiyyah), and the attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ) all serve to cultivate awe, to follow the pattern of grandeur, and to show, in what is evident, the kindness shown to him (ﷺ).

﴿In rows﴾, i.e., neither scattered nor mixed together. There is therefore no indication here of the unity of the row or its multiplicity. And it is reported in a sound hadith: "Allah will gather the first and the last in one plain, in rows" (ṣufūfan).

﴿Indeed you have come to Us﴾ is on the basis of an implied saying (idmar al-qawl), in a manner in which it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ʿuriḍū, meaning: "said to them", or "and We will say to them". As for its being the governing element of "the day We set the mountains in motion" (yawma nusayyiru), as has been said, it is far from the eloquence of the Glorious Revelation. How could it not be? For it would entail that this statement is the one primarily intended, to the exclusion of the other calamities, although it is specifically connected to what precedes it of the presentation and the gathering, and not to the moving of the mountains and the emergence of the earth.

﴿Just as We created you﴾ is an attribute of an implied verbal noun (maṣdar muqaddar), meaning: a coming like your coming at the time of Our creating you ﴿the first time﴾; or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in jitumūnā, meaning: existing as We created you the first time, barefoot, naked, uncircumcised; or nothing of what you used to boast of, of wealth and helpers, is with you. Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you have indeed come to Us alone, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾.

﴿Rather, you claimed that We would never appoint for you an appointed time﴾. It is a turning away (iḍrāb) and a transition from one statement to another, both for rebuke and reproach. That is: you claimed in the world that We would never ever appoint a time in which We would fulfil what We promised of resurrection and what follows it. The "an" here is the lightened form of the heavy one (an-mukhaffafah), separated from its predicate by the negative particle, because it is a verbal nominal clause that is active and not a supplication. The adverbial phrase is either a second object of "jaʿala" which means "to make", the first being "mawʿidan"; or a circumstantial clause from "mawʿid"; or it has the meaning of creating and originating.

﴿And the Book will be placed﴾: this is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿they will be presented﴾, and falls under the terrifying matters whose remembrance is intended by reminding of their time. It is expressed in the past tense, as is usual in such contexts, to indicate that it is certain to happen. That is, the scrolls of deeds will be placed. The singular noun is used because the genus (jins) suffices. Its placing may mean either that it is put into the hands of its owners, on the right or on the left, or that it is put into the scale (mīzān).

﴿So you will see the criminals﴾, all of them, so that the deniers of the Resurrection enter among them as a primary inclusion.

﴿fearful﴾, afraid ﴿of what is in it﴾, of the crimes and sins it contains, ﴿and they will say﴾, upon coming to know what is in its details, down to the smallest speck (naqīr) and the thinnest membrane (qiṭmīr).

﴿"Woe to us!"﴾, calling out for their own destruction, which they brought upon themselves from among all destructions, seeking it so that they would be annihilated and would not witness the horror of what they encounter. That is: "O woe to us, come forth, for this is the time of your presence."

﴿What is this Book?﴾, that is, what sort of thing is it? His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It leaves out nothing small or great but has counted it﴾, that is, it contains it. The phrase ﴿and has counted it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah) that confirms what is implied by the interrogative sentence of amazement, or it is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāfiyyah) built upon a question that arose from the amazement, as if it were said: "What is its condition that one should be amazed at it?" So it was answered: ﴿It leaves out no evil deed, small or great, but has counted it.﴾

﴿And they will find what they did﴾ in the world of evil deeds, or the recompense for what they did, ﴿present﴾, recorded and ready. ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾, so as to record deeds that were not done, or to increase the punishment they deserve. This is a demonstration of the justice (muʿdalah) of the eternal Pen.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 50:**

﴿And when We said to the angels﴾, i.e., remember the time when We said to them, ﴿"Prostrate yourselves before Adam"﴾, a prostration of greeting and honour, and its detail has already passed. ﴿So they prostrated﴾, all of them, in compliance with the command.

﴿Except Iblis﴾, for he did not prostrate; rather he refused and was arrogant. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"He was of the jinn"﴾ is a resumed statement (isti'naf) brought in the manner of a causal explanation (ta'lil) for what the exclusion of the accursed one from those who prostrated implies, as if it were said: "What was the matter with him that he did not prostrate?" So it was said: "His origin was that of a jinn."

﴿So he defied the command of his Lord﴾, i.e., he went out of obedience to Him, as the particle "fa" (so) indicates. Or it means he became a defiant disbeliever because of the command of Allah, exalted is He, for had it not been for that, he would not have refused. The mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya), which is incompatible with defiance, serves to show the complete ugliness of what he did. The purpose of recounting his story is to renew the rebuke against the arrogant who boast of their lineages and their wealth, and who disdain to be counted among the poor believers, by showing that this conduct is the work of Iblis, and that they, in it, follow his enticement, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿"Will you then take him..."﴾ etc. For the interrogative particle (hamza) is for denunciation and wonder, and the "fa" is for sequence, i.e., do you, after your knowledge of the emergence of those ugly deeds from him, take him [as a guardian]?

﴿And his offspring﴾, i.e., his children and his followers, who are called his offspring metaphorically. Qatada said: "They reproduce as the children of Adam reproduce." It was also said: "He inserts his tail into his posterior, and lays an egg from which a group of devils hatch."

﴿As protectors besides Me﴾, so that you would take them in place of Me and obey them instead of My obedience.

﴿While they﴾, i.e., while the state is that Iblis and his offspring ﴿are an enemy to you﴾, i.e., enemies to you both, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Indeed they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds"﴾, and His saying: ﴿"They are the enemy"﴾. This [use of the singular "enemy" for a plural] was done to make him resemble a verbal noun (masdar), like "qabul" (acceptance) and "wulu'" (eagerness). The restriction of the taking [as protectors] to a circumstantial clause (hal) is for emphasizing and intensifying the denunciation, for its content prevents the taking [of protectors] from occurring, and is absolutely incompatible with it.

﴿Evil is it as a substitute for the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., for those who place a thing in other than its proper place.

﴿A substitute﴾: Iblis and his offspring are a substitute from Allah, glorified is He. The shift to the third person (iltifat, i.e., the grammatical shift from address to absence) together with placing "the wrongdoers" in the position of the pronoun, indicates the announcement of complete wrath, and points to the fact that what they did is an evident, ugly wrong.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 51:

﴿I did not make them witnesses﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain that they do not deserve to be taken as such in themselves, after the obstacles to that have been explained, namely the baseness of their origin, their wickedness and their enmity. That is: I did not bring Iblis and his offspring to witness.

﴿the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, since I created them before creating those, ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾, that is: nor did I make some of them witness the creation of others, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾. This is what the majority have agreed upon, to avoid separating the two pronouns and to preserve the apparent wording of "themselves" (anfus). You may also return the second pronoun to the wrongdoers (zalimin) and adopt the separation, on the basis that the meaning is directed toward it. For the denial of the Satans' witnessing the creation of those whom they take as allies is what the denial of taking them as allies revolves around, on the basis that the least thing that makes taking someone as an ally valid is the presence of the ally at the creation of the one taken as ally, and where there is no presence there is definitely no valid basis for allegiance. As for the denial of some of the Satans witnessing the creation of others among them, it has nothing to do with the pivot of the aforementioned denial. Moreover, if some of them witnessing the creation of others were a valid basis for the witness's allegiance, on the basis that it indicates his perfection in that he has a share in the creation of the witnessed in general, it would still undermine the witnessed's allegiance, on the basis of his deficiency relative to the one whose creation he witnessed. Thus the denial of the mentioned witnessing does not purely consist in denying the perfection that validates allegiance from all, and the criterion for the mentioned denial.

﴿Nor would I take the misleaders﴾, that is: taking them. The explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to blame them, to record their misguidance upon them, and to emphasize the earlier denial of taking them as allies.

﴿as helpers (ʿaḍudan)﴾: helpers in the matter of creation, or in some matter of Mine, so that one might suppose their partnership in allegiance on the basis of a share in some attributes of lordship. In this there is mockery of them and a notice of the complete feebleness of their intellects and the flimsiness of their opinions, since they do not grasp this clear matter, which is hardly confused even by the foolish and children, so that they would need to have it stated explicitly. The choice of denying their witnessing rather than denying their being witnesses, and of denying their being taken as helpers rather than denying that they are such, is to indicate that they are subdued under His power, subject to His will and determination concerning them, and that they are far from deserving witnessing or aid from their own accord, without being brought to witness or taken. The utmost that might be supposed concerning them is that they reach that level by the command of Allah, mighty and majestic, and that has hardly come to pass. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and the meaning is: I did not make them witness the creation of that, nor did I inform them of the secrets of creation, nor did I single them out with virtues that others do not possess so that they would be exemplars for people, who would then believe by their belief, as they claim. Thus their words are not heeded in hope of their support for the religion, for it is not fitting for Me to seek help from misleaders. This is supported by the reading with a fatha on the ta', addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the meaning is: it is not proper for you to seek help from them, and describing them as misleaders serves as the reason for denying the taking. It is also read: (muttakhidha) "al-mudilliyn" in accordance with the original. It is also read: ('udhdan) with a damma on the ʿayn and a sukun on the ḍad, and with a fatha and sukun, by lightening, and with two dammas by assimilation, and with two fathas as the plural of ʿadid, like rasad and rasid.

And [mention] the Day when He says, meaning God, mighty and majestic, to the disbelievers, as a rebuke and a demonstration of their helplessness. It is also recited with the *nūn al-ʿaẓama* (the plural of majesty, the "we" form): ﴿Call on My partners whom you claimed﴾ to be your intercessors, so that they would intercede for you. What is meant by them is everything that was worshipped besides Him, exalted is He. It has also been said that they are Iblīs and his offspring.

﴿So they called upon them﴾, that is, they called on them for help. This shows how eagerly they relied on them to intercede for them, since it is known that there was no way to repel the punishment.

﴿But they did not respond to them﴾: they did not help them, since that was not possible. Stating this, although it is obvious, carries a mockery of them, and indicates that they are so foolish that they will not understand it unless it is stated explicitly.

﴿And We placed between them﴾, between those who call and those who are called upon, ﴿a barrier of destruction﴾. *Mawbiqan* is either a noun of place, or a verbal noun from *wabaqa wubūqan*, like *wathaba wuthūban*, or *wabiqa wabaqan*, like *faraḥa faraḥan*, meaning "he perished". It means a place of destruction in which they share, which is the Fire. Or it means enmity which, in its severity, is itself destruction, like the saying of ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him: "Let not your love be excessive, nor your hatred destructive." It has also been said that *al-bayn* means connection, so the meaning is: We made their association in this world a destruction for them in the Hereafter. It is also permissible that by the partners are meant the angels, ʿUzayr, ʿĪsā and Maryam, peace be upon them, and by *al-mawbiq* is meant a vast separating barrier, that is: We placed between them a great distance in which the years would be spent, because of the extreme remoteness between them, for they are at the bottom of Hell while they are in the highest of the Gardens.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 53:

﴿And the criminals will see the Fire﴾. The apparent noun (al-muzhar) is placed in the position of the pronoun (al-mudmar), to make explicit their criminality and to censure them for it.

﴿So they will think﴾, that is, "so they will be certain" (fa-ayqanu), ﴿that they are about to fall into it﴾, meaning they are about to be immersed in it and fall therein; or they thought, when they saw it from a far place, that they were about to fall into it right then.

﴿And they will not find a way of turning away from it﴾, meaning a turning aside (insirafan), or a place of refuge (ma'adilan) to which they could turn.

﴿And We have certainly varied﴾, that is, We repeated and presented [it] in many forms of arrangement (*nazm*, the composition of the text).

﴿in this Qur'an for the people﴾, for their benefit and advantage.

﴿from every kind of example﴾: from within it is what has passed of the example of the two men and the example of the life of this world; or [it means] from every type of the wondrous meanings that call to faith, which are in their strangeness, their beauty, and their power to attract the soul, like the example, so that they might receive it with acceptance, but they did not do so.

﴿And man is, by his nature, the most contentious of things﴾, that is, the most of the things from which contention arises. Here it means intense quarrelling in falsehood and dispute, from *jadal*, which is twisting. *Mujadalah* (debate) is *mulawah*, because each of the two debaters twists against the other. Its case ending (*intisab*) is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification of the noun), and the meaning is that his contention is greater than the contention of any [other] disputant.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 55:

﴿And what prevented the people﴾ i.e., the people of Makkah, whose falsehoods have been related.

﴿from believing﴾ i.e., from believing in God the Exalted and abandoning the polytheism they were engaged in.

﴿when the guidance came to them﴾ i.e., the great Qur'an, which guides to faith through its various kinds of meanings that necessitate it.

﴿and seeking forgiveness from their Lord﴾ for the sins of various kinds they had committed (p-230), among which is their disputing with falsehood against the truth. ﴿Except that the way of the former peoples should come upon them﴾ i.e., except seeking that their way (sunnah) come upon them, or except awaiting its coming, or except its estimation, so the modifier (al-mudaf) was deleted and the modified-to (al-mudaf ilayh) was placed in its position. Their way (sunnah) is annihilation (al-isti'sal).

﴿Or the punishment come upon them﴾ i.e., the punishment of the Hereafter.

﴿face to face﴾ i.e., in kinds. It is the plural of qabil, or "face to face" (i'anan) as in the reading qibalan with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', and it was also read with two fathas, meaning "in front of them" (mustaqbalan). It is said: "I met him qubulan, qabalan and qibalan." Its accusative status is as a circumstantial (haliyyah) from the pronoun, or from "the punishment." The meaning is that what the noble Qur'an contains of matters that necessitate faith is such that, were it not for such strong wisdom, people would not have refrained from faith, even though they are disposed to excessive disputation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 56:

﴿And We do not send the messengers﴾ to the nations except as those who are associated with some state of affairs, ﴿except﴾ in the state of being ﴿bringers of good news﴾ to the believers of reward, ﴿and warners﴾ to the disbelievers and the sinners of punishment.

﴿And those who disbelieve dispute with falsehood﴾ by demanding signs after the appearance of miracles, and by asking about the story of the People of the Cave and the like, out of obstinacy, ﴿in order to refute thereby﴾, that is, by the disputation, ﴿the truth﴾, that is, to remove it from its place and to nullify it, from "idhdaḥ al-qadam" (the slipping of the foot), which is its sliding. This is their saying to the messengers, peace and blessings be upon them: "You are only human beings like us, and if God had willed, He would have sent down angels," and the like of these.

﴿And they take My signs﴾, which mountains would crumble before.

﴿And [what] they are warned of﴾, that is, what they were warned of: the dreadful calamities announcing punishment and torment upon them, or their warning itself.

﴿in mockery﴾, as ridicule. It was also read with the letter zay (ز) unvoweled as "huzu", which is that by which one is mocked.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 57:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord﴾, meaning the Great Qur'an.

﴿But turns away from them﴾, and does not reflect upon them, nor is admonished by them. This construction, although its conventional denotation is the negation of being the most unjust, without any reference to negating equality in injustice, its customary understanding is that he is more unjust than every unjust person. The attribution of being most unjust to what lies within the relative clause, namely turning away from the Qur'an, serves to indicate that the injustice of one who disputes it and takes it in mockery is beyond all bounds.

﴿And forgets what his hands have sent forward﴾, that is, his deeds of disbelief and disobedience, among which is what was mentioned of disputing in falsehood and mocking the truth, and he did not consider their consequence.

﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, that is, many veils. It is the plural of kinan (kinan, "covering"), and it is a justification for their turning away and forgetting, in that they are sealed upon their hearts.

﴿Lest they understand it﴾ is an object of what the discourse indicates, meaning: We have prevented them from grasping its reality; or it is an object of purpose, meaning: lest they understand it (lest they understand it, from karahat an yafqahuhu, "out of aversion that they should understand it").

﴿And in their ears﴾, that is, We placed in them ﴿deafness﴾, a heaviness that prevents them from hearing it.

﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, then, ever﴾, that is, there will never be any guidance from them at all during the period of obligation. "Idhan" (then) is the answer to a condition, and a response to the question of the Prophet (ﷺ) implied by his utmost concern for their Islam, as if he (ﷺ) had said: "Why do I not call them?" So it was said: "If you call them..." etc. The pronoun referring to the relative pronoun in these five places is in the plural in view of its meaning, just as its singular form in the five preceding places is in view of its wording.

(p-231) ﴿And your Lord﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying, ﴿the Forgiving﴾, is its predicate (khabar). His saying, ﴿Possessor of mercy﴾, that is, the one described by it, is a predicate following a predicate. The mention of forgiveness in the intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha), rather than [the mention of] retribution (al-hurma), serves to draw attention to the abundance of sins, and because forgiveness is the abandonment of harms. He, glorified is He, is able to leave off an infinite amount of punishment, whereas mercy is an act and bringing-into-existence, and nothing enters under existence except what is finite. The first attribute is placed first either because clearing (al-takhliya) precedes adorning (al-tahliya), or because it is more important given the circumstance, since the context is one of explaining that the punishment is delayed from them after they have become deserving of it, as His saying, mighty and majestic is He, expresses: ﴿If He were to seize them﴾, that is, if He were to wish to seize them, ﴿for what they have earned﴾ of sins, among which is what is related of them concerning their disputing in falsehood, their turning away from the signs of their Lord, and their indifference to the destructive deeds they have committed.

﴿He would have hastened for them the punishment﴾, because their deeds deserved that, and the choice of the expression "seize" (mu'akhadha), which indicates the severity of seizing swiftly, over "punish" (al-ta'dhib) and "chastise" ('uquba) and the like, is to make known that the negation derived from the protasis of the conditional clause relates to the attribute of swiftness, as its consequent indicates. The choice of the future form, although the meaning is past, is to convey that the non-occurrence of the hastening of punishment for them is due to the continuing absence of the will to seize them, since the present-tense verb in the place of the past tense indicates the continuation of the negation of the action in what has passed, as has been verified in its proper place.

﴿Rather, for them is an appointed time﴾: a temporal noun (ism zaman), which is the Day of Badr or the Day of Resurrection. The sentence is conjoined to an implied element, as if it were said: "But they are not going to be seized suddenly." ﴿They will never find﴾ at all ﴿besides Him any refuge﴾ (maws), a shelter or a place of safety. It is said: wa'ala, meaning he was saved; and wa'ala ilayhi, meaning he took refuge in it.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 59:

﴿And those cities﴾ — that is, the cities of 'Ad, Thamud and their likes. It is a subject (mubtada') with an implied omitted noun (al-mudaf) in its construction, meaning: "and the people of those cities," whose predicate (khabar) is his saying, exalted is He: ﴿We destroyed them﴾. Or it is an object (maf'ul) of an implied verb that is explained by it, ﴿when they did wrong﴾, meaning: at the time of their wrongdoing, just as Quraysh did with the abominations related about them. The omission of the object is either for generalizing the wrongdoing, or for treating the verb as intransitive, meaning: when they committed wrongdoing. As for "lamma" (when/since): it is either a particle (harf), as Ibn 'Usfur said, or an adverb (zarf) used to express causation (ta'lil). The intended meaning is not a specific time in which they committed the wrongdoing, but a period extending from the beginning of the wrongdoing to its end.

﴿And We appointed for their destruction﴾ — that is, We fixed for their destruction ﴿an appointed time﴾ — that is, a specific time from which they have no escape. This is cited as evidence for what was done to Quraysh, namely the fixing of an appointed time, so that they may take heed and not be deceived by the delay of the punishment. It has also been read with a ḍammah on the mīm and a fatḥah on the lām, meaning: their destruction (ihlakuhum), and also read with fatḥah on both.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 60:

﴿And when Musa said﴾ It is in the accusative by an implied verb, i.e., "Remember the time when he, peace be upon him, said﴾ ﴿to his young man﴾ — and he is Yusha' ibn Nun ibn Afraim ibn Yusuf, peace be upon him. He was called his "fata" (young man, servant) because he would serve him and follow him. It is also said that he was learning from him, and a student is called a "fata" even if he is an elder. Perhaps the purpose of mentioning, right after the statement that for every nation there is an appointed time (mawid), the reminder of what is in the story concerning the appointed time of meeting, along with the other great benefits it contains.

﴿I will not cease﴾ From barah (to depart), of the defective kind, like zala yazal (to cease), i.e., "I will not cease to travel." The predicate is omitted, relying on the contextual indication (qarina al-hal), since this was at the time of setting out on the journey, and relying on what follows it in His saying: ﴿until I reach﴾, for that is a limit (ghaya) which calls for something having that limit which leads to it. It is also possible that the original sentence was "my journey will not cease to be in progress until I reach," so the genitive noun is deleted and the attached noun is put in its place, whereby the pronoun (in the genitive position) becomes a nominative concealed pronoun, and the verb changes from the third-person form to the first-person speech form. It is also possible that it is from barah in the complete sense, like zala yazul, i.e., "I will not depart from what I am intent upon until I reach﴿the meeting place of the two seas﴾." It is the meeting point of the Persian Sea and the Roman Sea on the eastern side. It is also said: Tangier. It is also said: they are the Kurr and the Rass in Armenia. It is also said: Ifriqiya. It has also been read with a kasra on the mim, like mashriq.

﴿Or I will journey for a long age﴾ I will travel for a long period of time, during which I am certain to miss the goal. Huqub means an age (dahr). Or eighty years. The origin of this resolve was that when Musa, peace be upon him, prevailed over Egypt together with the Children of Israel, and they settled there after the destruction of the Copts, Allah, mighty and majestic, commanded him to remind his people of the blessing. So he stood among them as a preacher with a marvelous sermon by which hearts softened and eyes shed tears. They said to him: Who is the most knowledgeable of people? He said: I am. So Allah, exalted, rebuked him because he did not refer knowledge back to Him, mighty and majestic, and He revealed to him: Rather, a servant of Mine at the meeting place of the two seas is more knowledgeable than you, and he is al-Khidr, peace be upon him. He was in the days of Afridun, before Musa, peace be upon him, and he was in the vanguard of Dhu al-Qarnayn the Great, and he remained until the days of Musa. It is also said: Musa, peace be upon him, asked his Lord: Which of Your servants is most beloved to You? He said: The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me. He said: Which of Your servants is most just? He said: The one who judges by the truth and does not follow desire. He said: Which of Your servants is most knowledgeable? He said: The one who seeks the knowledge of people to add to his knowledge, perhaps he will hit upon a word that guides him to guidance or turns him away from ruin. He said: If among Your servants there is one more knowledgeable than me, then guide me to him. He said: More knowledgeable than you is al-Khidr. He said: Where shall I seek him? He said: On the shore of the sea, at the rock. He said: O Lord, how can I find him? He said: Take a fish in a basket; wherever you lose it, he is there. So he took a fish and put it in a basket, and he said to his young man: When you lose the fish, inform me. So they set off walking.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 61:

﴿فَلَمّا بَلَغا﴾ [So when they both reached] The fa' (fa' fasiha, the "expressive" fa', which reveals an omitted condition) is as indicated above. ﴿مَجْمَعَ بَيْنِهِما﴾ [the meeting-place of the two of them]: i.e., the meeting-place of the two seas. "Baynihima" is an adverbial of place (zarf) which is attached to its object (idafa) by way of expansion (ittisa'), or it carries the sense of "junction" (wasl).

﴿نَسِيا حُوتَهُما﴾ [they forgot their fish], which was made the sign of finding the sought-after person by its disappearance; i.e., they forgot to check on its condition and what would happen to it. It was said: Yusha' forgot to bring it forward, and Musa, peace be upon him, forgot to instruct him concerning it with anything. It is narrated that when they both reached the meeting-place of the two seas, where there was the rock and the Spring of Life, whose water does not touch a dead thing except that it comes to life, they placed their heads on the rock and slept. When the coolness and refreshment of the water reached the fish, it came to life, and they had already eaten from it. This happened after Yusha' (peace be upon him) had awoken. It was also said: Musa (peace be upon him) performed ablution from that spring, so the water splashed onto the fish and it came to life and fell into the water.

﴿فاتَّخَذَ سَبِيلَهُ في البَحْرِ سَرَبًا﴾ [and it took its way into the sea, making a tunnel]: a passage like a sarab, which is a tunnel (nafaq). It was said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, held back the flow of the water over the fish, so it became like an arch over it, a miracle for Musa, or for al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. The accusative of "sarab" is as a second object of "ittakhadha," and "fi al-bahr" is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from it, or from "al-sabil"; it is also permissible for it to be connected to "ittakhadha."

﴿Then when they had passed on﴾, that is, the meeting place of the two seas, which had been appointed as the place of encounter. It was said: they set out by night. They travelled through the night and the next day until noon, and hunger afflicted Musa, peace be upon him. At that point ﴿he said to his young companion, "Bring us our morning meal"﴾, that is, that with which we may take our midday meal, which was the fish, as the reply indicates.

﴿Indeed we have met with fatigue from this journey of ours﴾. (p-233) This refers to what they travelled after passing the appointed place. ﴿Fatigue﴾ means weariness and exhaustion. It was said: he had not been tired and had not been hungry before that. The clause is in the position of a causal explanation for the command to bring the meal, either on the basis that exhaustion arises only from the weakness caused by hunger, or on the basis of the rest that is obtained during the meal.

**"He said"**: that is, his young companion (*fata*), upon him be peace.

﴿Did you see when we took refuge at the rock?﴾ That is, we sought shelter by it and stayed beside it. Mentioning the taking of refuge at the rock, although what was mentioned earlier was twice reaching the meeting place of the two seas, serves to specify the location of the incident more precisely, since the meeting place is a wide area in which it would not be possible to pin down the intended event by attributing it to that area alone. It also serves to prepare an excuse, for taking refuge by the rock and sleeping beside it are things that ordinarily lead to forgetfulness. "Seeing" is used metaphorically for complete knowledge and full observation. The interrogative is intended to express Moses' (peace be upon him) amazement at the forgetfulness that had befallen him there, given that what he had witnessed was among the great wonders that are hardly ever forgotten. His losing it was made a sign of finding what he sought, and this is a common way of speaking among people. One of them says to his companion when a calamity befalls him: "Did you see what has befallen me?", meaning by it to magnify the matter and to make his companion marvel at it, since it is something not known to occur. It is not a genuine request for information, as has been said. The object is omitted, relying on what is indicated by the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, I forgot the fish﴾. In this there is an emphasis on the amazement and an inducement to regard the forgotten matter as great. The forgetting is attributed to the name "the fish" rather than to the pronoun referring to the food, although the food is what he was commanded to bring. This is to alert from the outset that it is not like the forgetfulness of a traveller about his provisions at a halting place, and that what he witnessed does not belong to the category of matters connected with food insofar as it is food and provision, but rather insofar as it is a fish like the rest of the fishes, with an additional feature. That is: I forgot to mention to you its matter and the wondrous things I witnessed from it.

﴿And none made me forget it except Satan﴾ by his preoccupying whispering that distracted me from that. The words of the Exalted, ﴿that I mention it﴾, are a *badal ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion, a grammatical term for a substitute that encompasses a part or aspect of what it replaces) for the pronoun, meaning: none made me forget to mention it to you. Attaching the forgetting first to the pronoun referring to the fish, and then mentioning it explicitly, in the manner of substitution, which signals the setting aside of what is replaced, indicates that the true object of the forgetting is also not the fish itself but the mention of its matter. It has been read as "*an adhkurahu*". Choosing *an adhkurahu* (a verbal clause with "that") over the verbal noun is for emphasis, since the verbal noun denotes the event itself at the moment of its occurrence. Although the situation is strange and its forgetting is not usual, it was nevertheless because Moses (peace be upon him) had become accustomed to witnessing its like and had grown familiar with it that his concern to preserve it diminished.

﴿And it took its way into the sea, a marvel﴾ is an explanation of one aspect of the matter of the fish, indicating another aspect of it, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause placed before it for the sake of giving attention to the excuse. It is as if it were said: it came to life and moved, fell into the sea, and took for itself a wondrous path therein. So "a marvel" is the second object of *ittakhadha* (took), and the adverbial phrase is a circumstantial clause relating to one of the two objects, or to the second. Or the second object is "a marvel," being an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a wondrous taking, which is the nature of its course being like a tunnel and a subterranean channel. Or it is the verbal noun of an omitted verb, meaning: I marvel at it greatly. It has been said that this is from the words of Moses (upon him be prayers and peace), but that is not the correct view.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 64:

﴿Qāla﴾ i.e., Musa, upon him be peace, said: ﴿That﴾, which you mentioned concerning the matter of the fish.

﴿"Mā kunna (p-234) nabghi"﴾ It is also read with the ya' affirmed (nabghī). The pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) is omitted; its original form is nabghīhi, i.e., "we seek it, because it is a sign of attaining the desired goal." ﴿Fa-artadda﴾ i.e., they returned ﴿upon their traces﴾, the path by which they had come ﴿qaṣaṣan﴾, retracing (yaqussāni qaṣaṣan), i.e., following their traces by following, or "retracing [their steps] until they reached the rock."

﴿So they found a servant from among Our servants﴾ The indefiniteness (*al-tankir*, the use of a noun without the definite article, here عَبْدًا, "a servant") is for magnification, and the attribution (*al-idafah*, the possessive construction, here مِن عِبادِنا, "from among Our servants") is for honour. The majority hold that he is al-Khidr, and his name is Balya ibn Malkan. It is said that he is al-Yasa', and it is said that he is Ilyas, upon them be prayers and peace.

﴿We had given him mercy from Us﴾ This is revelation and prophethood, as the indefiniteness of "mercy" (رَحْمَةً) suggests, and its being specific to the Presence of Majesty.

﴿And taught him knowledge from Our own presence﴾ A special knowledge whose essence cannot be fully grasped and whose extent cannot be measured, and it is the knowledge of the unseen.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 67:

﴿Qāla﴾ i.e., al-Khidr: ﴿Innaka lan tastaṭīʿa maʿiya ṣabrā﴾ ("Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me"). He negated from him the ability to be patient in his company in an emphatic manner, as if it were something that is not valid and cannot be sound, and he gave the reason for it with his saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 68:

﴿And how can you have patience regarding that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾ This is an announcement that he (al-Khidr) undertakes affairs whose underlying purpose is hidden and whose outward appearances are objectionable, and a righteous man, especially the bearer of a Sharia (law), cannot restrain himself from recoiling when witnessing them.
