In the Sahih of al-Bukhari (a collection of hadith compiled by Imam al-Bukhari): "al-Khidr said: 'O Musa, I am upon a knowledge from the knowledge of Allah, Most High, which He taught me and which you do not know, and you are upon a knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which Allah taught you and which I do not know.'" And khubran (in knowledge) is a tamyiz (specification of the noun), meaning: your report has not encompassed it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 69:

﴿Said﴾ Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿You will find me, God willing, patient﴾ with you, not objecting to you. The placement of the exception (istithna') between the two objects of "finding" (wijdan) is for the sake of fully emphasizing the seeking of blessing (tayammun), and so that it is not supposed that it is connected to "patient."

﴿And I will not disobey any command of yours﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to "patient," meaning: you will find me patient and not disobedient. In promising this "finding" there is an emphasis that is not present in promising patience itself and abstaining from disobedience alone. Or it is conjoined to "you will find me," in which case it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). The first is preferable for what you have come to know, and because its connection to the exception is then evident. In this there is evidence that the actions of servants occur by the will of God, glorified and exalted be He.

"He said: "If you follow me, then do not question me about anything until I myself mention it to you."

This is permission to follow him after the two previous attempts (the "first" and the "second" [occasions]). The fa' (then) introduces the conditional consequence of what came before, namely Musa's (peace be upon him) commitment to patience and obedience.

﴿So do not question me about anything﴾ that you witness of my actions; that is, do not open with questions about its wisdom, let alone dispute or object to it.

﴿Until I mention to you its explanation﴾ That is, until I begin to explain it. This indicates that whatever proceeds from him has wisdom and a wholly praiseworthy end, and this is part of the etiquette of the student toward the scholar, and of the follower toward the one he follows. It is also recited as (falā tasalannī) with the emphatic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd al-muthaqqalah)."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 71:

﴿So they set out⦈ i.e., Musa and al-Khadir, upon them be prayer and peace, along the shore, seeking a ship. As for Yusha', Musa, upon him be prayer and peace, had sent him off to the Children of Israel. It is said: they passed by a ship and spoke to its people, and they recognised al-Khadir, so they carried them both without a fare.

﴿Until when they boarded the ship⦈ The use of the verb "rakiba" (to board/ride) in such contexts with the preposition "fi" (in), while in other places it is used without it, as in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿that you may ride upon them, and as adornment﴾, follows what its transitivity by itself requires, for the reason we indicated in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he said, "Board therein"﴾, and not because of what has been said, that riding in it carries the meaning of entering.

﴿He made a hole in it⦈ It is said: he made a hole in it after they had become entangled in the sea, when he took an axe and pulled out two planks from its boards on the side toward the water. At that point ﴿he (Musa) said⦈, upon him be peace: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people?⦈ From "al-ighraq" (to drown). It is also read with the doubled letter, from "al-taghriq" (to cause to sink), and "liyaghraqa ahluha" from the triliteral form.

﴿Indeed you have done⦈ "ji'ta": you came, and you did.

﴿a grave thing (shay'an imra)⦈ i.e., a great, dreadful matter, from "amira al-amr" when the matter became great. It is said the original was "imran," and it was lightened.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 72:

﴿He said﴾ i.e., al-Khidr, peace be upon him.

﴿Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ It is a reminder of what he had said before, and an affirmation of its content, containing a rebuke for not keeping his promise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 73:

﴿He said: "Do not take me to task for what I forgot"﴾ — by my forgetting, or for the thing I forgot, or for something I forgot, namely his instruction not to ask him about the wisdom of the actions that proceeded from him, whose causes were hidden, before he explained them. He meant that he had forgotten his instruction. There is no blame upon the one who forgets, as is related in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, that the first [objection] was from Musa out of forgetfulness. Or he spoke in the mode of a prohibition against being taken to task for forgetfulness, which gives the impression that he had forgotten, so as to extend his excuse for the denial; this is among the figurative expressions (ma'arid al-kalam) by which one guards against lying while attaining the aim. Or he meant by forgetting "leaving", i.e.: do not take me to task for what I left of your instruction the first time.

﴿And do not burden me﴾ — i.e., do not overwhelm me, and do not impose upon me.

﴿for my affair﴾ — and that is following him.

﴿with difficulty﴾ — i.e., do not make my following you difficult for me, and make it easy for me by overlooking and refraining from questioning. It was also read: ﴿ʿusuran﴾ (عُسُرًا) with two dammas.

(p-236) ﴿So they set off.﴾ The *fa'* here is *fasihah* (an eloquent *fa'* that signals an implied omitted clause). The meaning is: he accepted his excuse, so they left the ship and set off.

﴿Until, when they met a boy, he killed him.﴾ It was said: the boy was playing with other boys, and he broke his neck. It was also said: he struck his head against the wall. And it was said: he laid him down and slaughtered him with a knife.

﴿He said﴾, that is, Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿Have you killed a pure soul, not in retaliation for another soul?﴾ "Pure" means free from sins. It is also recited as *zakiyah* (a variant reading). ﴿Not in retaliation for another soul﴾ means not in retaliation for killing a soul that is forbidden to kill. The specific mention of the negation of this permitting cause, out of all the other permitting causes (apostasy after faith, and adultery after being *muhsan*, i.e., married and chaste), is because it is the most likely to occur given the boy's condition. Perhaps the change in the noble wording, by placing what came from Khidr (peace be upon him) here within the conditional clause (*shart*), and by bringing out what came from Musa (peace be upon him) in the form of the consequent (*jaza'*) whose benefit is intended, is because the one truly worthy of this would be what came from Khidr (peace be upon him) of wondrous extraordinary acts (*khawariq*). This is because the soul yearns to hear its report, given how rarely such things occur in reality and how rarely news of them reaches minds. For this reason that point was observed in the first conditional clause, since the extraordinary acts that issued from him (peace be upon him) went out, by their occurring once, in the manner of a habit. So the soul turned away from expecting them and toward expecting the states of Musa (peace be upon him). Will he maintain the observance of his condition, by the requirement of his firm promise, upon witnessing another extraordinary act, or will he hasten to object? As occurred the first time, the intent was to convey what issued from him (peace be upon him), so he did what he did. How excellent is the matter of the revelation! As for what has been said, that killing is more hideous and objecting to it is more fitting, so that it would be right to make it the main point of the discourse, this is not a removal of the doubt at all; rather it supports it. The fact that killing is more hideous is among the reasons it rarely issues from a sensible believer, and why news of it rarely reaches the ears. That calls for making it a matter intended in itself. And that objecting to it is more fitting is among the reasons for its frequent issuing from every sensible person, and that does not require making it so.

﴿You have certainly done a terrible thing (*shay'an nukra*).﴾ It was said: its meaning is that it is more reprehensible than the first, since it cannot be remedied as the first could be remedied by repairing (the wall), and the like. It was also said: the matter is greater than a *nukra* (a reprehensible act), because killing one soul is less severe than drowning the people of the ship.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 75:

﴿He said: Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ The added emphasis (zīda lak) is for the increased rebuke for rejecting the stipulation (waṣiyya), and for the lack of steadiness and patience, since disgust and disapproval had been repeated from him, and he did not desist when reminded, until he intensified the reproach the second time.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 76:

﴿Qāla﴾ i.e., Musa, upon him be peace.

﴿In sa'altuka 'an shay'in ba'dahā﴾ i.e., after this time, ﴿fa-lā tuṣāhibnī﴾. It is also read in the form of if'āl (tuṣḥibnī), meaning: do not make me your companion.

﴿Qad balaghta min ladunnī 'udhran﴾ i.e., you have indeed given an excuse, and you have found from my side an excuse, since I opposed you three times. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "May Allah have mercy on my brother Musa; he was modest, so he said that. Had he remained with his companion, he would have seen the most wondrous of wonders." And it is read "ladunnī" with the nun lightened (ladunī), and it is read with the dal pronounced with sukūn, like ʿaḍd in ʿaḍud.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 77:

﴿So they set out, until when they came to the people of a town⟩ It is Antakya. It was also said: Ayla, which is the farthest land of God from the sky. It was also said: it is Barqa. It was also said: it is a town in al-Andalus. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "They were a people of a town who were base (li'am)." It was also said: the worst of towns is the one in which the guest is not hosted, and the right of the traveler (ibn al-sabil) is not recognized. His words, exalted is He: ﴿and asked them for food⟩ are in the genitive position as an attribute (sifah) of "town" (qaryah). Perhaps the shift from "asking them for food" to making it an attribute of "people" (ahl) is to intensify their condemnation for their evil conduct, for refusing hospitality is more odious and shameful when those who refuse are its own residents who dwell in it. It is narrated that they went around the town, asked them for food, and they did not feed them; and they asked them for hospitality, ﴿but they refused to entertain them⟩. Read with the doubled letter (tashdid), and it was also read with the single letter (takhfif) from ida'fah (hospitality). It is said: "dayafahu" when he had him as a guest; "adafahu" and "dayyafahu" mean he housed him and made him his guest. The literal meaning of "dafa" is "to incline toward," from "dafa al-sahm 'an al-gharad" (the arrow deviated from the target). Its counterpart is "zarahu," from "al-izwiraar" (turning away).

﴿And they found in it a wall about to collapse⟩ That is, it was near to falling. The word "irada" (wanting) is borrowed to express imminence, to indicate exaggeration in that. Al-infiqad means hastening in falling, and it is an infi'al form from "qadd" (to cut). It is said: "qadadtuhu fa-nqadda" (I cut it and it was cut), and from it comes "inqidad al-tayr wa al-kawkab" (the swooping of a bird and a star) for its falling swiftly. It was also said: it is an if'ilal form from "naqd" (breaking), like "ihmarra" from "al-humrah" (redness). It was read as ﴿yanqada⟩ from "naqd," and as ﴿yanqada⟩ from "inqaada al-sinn," when the tooth split lengthwise.

﴿So he set it upright⟩ It was said: he rubbed it with his hand and it stood. It was said: he demolished it and rebuilt it. It was said: he propped it up with a pillar he set beneath it. It was said: its height was one hundred cubits.

﴿He said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."⟩ As an incitement to him to accept a reward so that they might be sustained by it, or as an implicit reproach that his work was superfluous, due to the negation implied in "law." It is as if, when he saw their deprivation, the touch of need, and his occupation with what did not concern him, he could no longer restrain his patience. "Ittakhadha" (to take) is the form "ifta'ala" from "takhidha" in the sense of "akhadha" (to take), like "ittaba'a" from "taba'a." According to the Basrans, it is not from "akhadha." It was read as ﴿latakhidhta⟩, meaning "la-akhadhta" (you would have taken). It was also read with the assimilation of the dhal into the ta'.

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said), i.e., al-Khiḍr, upon him be peace.

﴿Hādhā firāqu baynī wa-baynik﴾ (This is parting between me and you). The verbal noun (maṣdar, "verbal noun") *firāq* is annexed to the adverbial noun (ẓarf, "adverb of time or place") *bayn* by way of extension (ittisā'an). It has also been read in its original form, *firāqu baynī wa-baynik* with *bayn* in the accusative. The thing indicated (al-mushār ilayhi) may be either the parting itself, as in the phrase *hādhā akhūka* ("this is your brother"), or the present time, meaning "this time is a time of parting between me and you," or the third question, meaning "this is the cause of that parting, according to what was promised."

﴿Sa-unabbi'uka﴾ (I will inform you). The *sīn* is for emphasis, indicating that the informing is not delayed.

﴿Bi-ta'wīli mā lam tastaṭi' 'alayhi ṣabran﴾ (with the ta'wīl (ultimate consequence) of that which you could not bear with patience). *Ta'wīl* means returning a thing to its final outcome (ma'āl). The word here means the outcome and final result, since what is informed of is the ta'wīl and not the interpretation itself. It refers to the deliverance of the ship from the grasp of the unjust king, the deliverance of the boy's parents from his evil together with receiving a better replacement, and the extraction of the treasure belonging to the two orphans. Placing the relative clause to express Musa's, upon him be peace, inability to be patient, rather than saying *bi-ta'wīli mā fa'altu* ("with the ta'wīl of what I did") or *bi-ta'wīli mā ra'ayta* ("with the ta'wīl of what you saw") and the like, contains a kind of indirect reproach (ta'rīḍ) and rebuke ('itāb) directed at him, upon him be peace.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 79:

﴿As for the boat﴾, which I damaged, ﴿it belonged to poor people﴾, weak people who could not resist the oppressors. It was also said: it belonged to ten brothers, five of whom were disabled and five of whom ﴿worked on the sea﴾. Attributing the work to all of them then is by way of predominance (al-taghlib), or because the work of agents is as the work of those who appointed them.

﴿So I wished to damage it﴾, that is, to make it defective.

﴿And behind them was a king﴾, that is, in front of them (amamahum), and it has been read with this meaning, or "behind them" (khalfahum). Their return would inevitably be past him. His name was Julanda ibn Karkar, and it was also said: Mintawala ibn Julanda al-Azdi.

﴿who seized every boat﴾, that is, every sound one, and it has been read thus as well.

﴿by force﴾ from its owners. Its accusative case is because it is a verbal noun (masdar) specifying the type of seizing. Perhaps the placing of the intention to damage the boat after the poverty of its owners, before explaining the fear of seizure, although both matters are its basis, is for the sake of giving attention to its matter, since it is the one that needs interpretation (ta'wil), and to indicate that the stronger of the two in being the basis is the first matter. For this reason, he is not concerned with rescuing the boats of other people even though the fear of seizure is also realized concerning them, and because delaying creates a separation between the boat and its pronoun, with the possibility of its reference being understood as to the nearest noun.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 80:

﴿As for the boy﴾, the one I killed, ﴿his parents were believers﴾. He did not explicitly mention their disbelief or his own, as an indication that there was no need to mention it since it was apparent.

﴿So We feared that he would burden them﴾, that is, we feared that he would overwhelm the two believing parents ﴿with tyranny﴾ against them, ﴿and disbelief﴾ in their blessing, through his disobedience and evil conduct, and that he would bring upon them evil and affliction. Or he would join his own tyranny and disbelief to their faith, so that two believers and a tyrannical disbeliever would be gathered in one house. Or he would infect them with his ailment and mislead them with his misguidance, so that they would apostatize because of him. The Khidr, upon him be peace, feared this from him only because Allah, glory be to Him, informed him of his condition and made him aware of the secret of his affair. It was read: (﴿so your Lord desired﴾), meaning: He, glory be to Him, disliked it in the manner of one who fears the bad outcome of a matter, so He changed it. It is also possible that the well-known reading is in the mode of narration, with the meaning: "so We disliked," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That I may give you﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 81:

﴿So We intended that their Lord should replace them with one better than him⦆ in purity, by granting them in his place a child better than him ﴿in purity﴾ — and in the mention of the title "Lordship" (rububiyya) and in its attribution to the two of them there is an indication, which is not hidden, of the intention that good should reach them — ﴿purity﴾, meaning cleansing from sins and bad character traits.

﴿And nearer in compassion﴾, meaning in mercy and tenderness. It has been said: a female child was born to them, whom a prophet married, and she bore a prophet through whose hands God Most High guided a nation of the nations. It has also been said: she bore seventy prophets. It has been said too: He replaced them with a believing son like them. It is also read as (yubaddiluhuma) with the doubled letter, and it is read as (ruhuman) with a damma on the ha' as well, and its accusative case is as a specification (tamyiz), like (zakatan).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 82:

﴿As for the wall﴾ (the one in question), ﴿it belonged to two orphan boys in the city﴾. It is the village mentioned earlier. Perhaps the reference to it as a "city" is to show a certain esteem for it, on account of the two orphans and their righteous father within it. It is said: their names were Asram and Sarim, and the name of the one who was killed was Jaysur.

﴿Beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾, of silver and gold, as has been related in a marfu' report. The condemnation of their hoarding in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿those who hoard gold and silver﴾ applies to one who does not pay their zakat and their other rights. It is also said that it was a tablet of gold on which was written: "I am amazed at the one who believes in destiny, how can he grieve? I am amazed at the one who believes in provision, how can he toil? I am amazed at the one who believes in death, how can he rejoice? I am amazed at the one who believes in reckoning, how can he be heedless? I am amazed at the one who knows the world and its turning over its people, how can he be at peace with it? There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." And it is said: (p-239) it was scrolls containing knowledge. ﴿Their father was righteous﴾: this is a notice that their being protected and their treasure being preserved was due to his righteousness. It is said: between them and the father in whose merit they were protected there were seven generations.

﴿So your Lord willed﴾, i.e., your Owner and the Manager of your affairs. The attribution of "Lord" to the pronoun of Musa, peace be upon him, rather than to the pronoun of the two boys, is a notice to him, peace be upon him, of the necessity of complete submission and surrender to His will, glorified is He, and of the obligation to avoid objecting to the matters that occurred in accordance with it, which were mentioned.

﴿That they should reach their maturity﴾, i.e., their full strength and the perfection of their judgment, ﴿and extract﴾ entirely ﴿their treasure﴾ from beneath the wall. Had I not repaired it, it would have collapsed, and the treasure would have come out from beneath it before they became capable of guarding the wealth and developing it, and it would have been lost.

﴿A mercy from your Lord﴾: a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative, i.e., "as those who were shown mercy by Him, the Mighty and Majestic," or an object of purpose, or an emphatic verbal noun for "willed," since the will for good is itself mercy. It is also said that it is connected to a suppressed verb, i.e., "I did what I did of the matters that you witnessed as a mercy from your Lord," and the attribution of "Lord" to the pronoun of the addressee rather than to the pronoun of the two boys supports this. Then the words of the Mighty and Exalted, ﴿and I did it not of my own accord﴾, i.e., not by my own opinion or effort, serve as an emphasis for this.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the consequences arranged within the thread of explanation, and the sense of distance in it is to indicate the elevated rank of those consequences in grandeur.

﴿The interpretation of that about which you could not be patient﴾, i.e., you were not able to be patient. The omission of the "ta'" is for lightness.

﴿Upon it with patience﴾: among the matters which troubled you, i.e., its outcome and its consequence. It then constitutes the fulfilment of the promised notification, or refers to the explanation itself, so the interpretation is in its meaning. In any case, it is a summary of what preceded, and in making the relative clause the very same as what passed there is a repetition for the sake of the indefinite and an intensification of the reproach.

Notice: The scholars differed concerning the life of al-Khidr, peace be upon him. It is said that he is alive, and the reason for this is that he was in the vanguard of Dhu al-Qarnayn; when he entered the darkness, al-Khidr came upon the Spring of Life, descended, bathed in it, and drank of its water, while Dhu al-Qarnayn mistook the way and returned. They said: Ilyas too is alive, and the two meet every year at the season. It is also said that he is dead, due to what has been related: "The Prophet ﷺ prayed the night prayer one night and then said: 'Do you see this night of yours? At the end of a hundred years from it, no one who is upon the face of the earth today will remain.' Had al-Khidr been alive at that time, he would not have lived beyond a hundred years." It is related that when Musa, peace be upon him, wished to part from him, he said: "Advise me." He said: "Do not seek knowledge in order to converse about it, but seek it in order to act upon it."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 83:

﴿They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn.﴾ They are the Jews. They asked him as a test, or Quraysh asked him at their prompting. The present tense (yas'aluna) indicates their continuing to ask until the answer comes. He is Dhu al-Qarnayn the Elder, whose name was Iskandar ibn Faylafus the Greek (al-Iskandar). Ibn Ishaq said: his name was Marzuban ibn Mardabah, of the descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh, peace be upon him, and he was black. It is also said: his name was Abd Allah ibn al-Dahhak. It is said: Mus'ab ibn Abd Allah ibn Fayman ibn Mansur ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Azar ibn Awn ibn Zayd ibn Kahlan ibn Saba' ibn Ya'rib ibn Qahtan. Al-Suhayli said: it is said that his name was Marzuban ibn Mudrikah, as mentioned by Ibn Hisham. He was the first of the Tubba'. It is also said that he was Afridun ibn al-Nu'man, who killed al-Dahhak. Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni mentioned in his book called al-Athar al-Baqiyah 'an al-Qurun al-Khaliyah that Dhu al-Qarnayn was Abu Karib, called Ibn Ayrin ibn Afriqis al-Himyari, and that his kingdom reached the east and west of the earth. He is the one whom the Tubba' of Yemen boasted of when he said:

Dhu al-Qarnayn was my grandfather, a Muslim, a king who rose high in the land, not disparaged,
He reached the east and the west, seeking the means of an affair from a wise, guiding one.

This view is closer, because the Adhwa' were from Yemen, such as Dhu al-Manar, Dhu Nuwas, Dhu al-Nun, Dhu (p-240) Ru'ayn, Dhu Yazan, and Dhu Jadan. Imam al-Razi said: the first view is the more apparent, because the one whose kingdom reached the extent and power described by the Glorious Revelation is none other than Alexander the Greek, as the history books attest. It is reported that when his father died he united the kingdom of the Romans, which had been divided into factions. Then he marched against the kings of the Arabs and conquered them. Then he pressed on until he reached the Green Sea. Then he returned to Egypt and built Alexandria, naming it after himself. Then he entered al-Sham and headed for the Children of Israel, arriving at Jerusalem, and slaughtered at its altar. Then he turned to Armenia and the Gate of Gates, and the Iraqis, the Copts, and the Berbers submitted to him. Then he headed toward the house of the son of Dara, defeated him repeatedly until his bodyguard killed him, and seized the realms of the Persians. He went to India and conquered it, and built the city of Sarandib and other great cities. Then he went to China and raided distant nations, and returned to Khurasan, where he built many cities. Then he returned to Iraq, fell ill at Shahrazur, and died. End of the Imam's words. It is related that the astrologers told him: "You will not die except on a land of iron, under a sky of wood." He used to bury the treasure of every town he entered and write it down with its description and location. He reached Babylon and had a nosebleed and fell from his mount. Shields were spread for him and he lay on them, but the sun harmed him, so they shaded him with a shield. He looked and said: "This is a land of iron and a sky of wood," and he became certain of death, and died. He was 1,600 years old. It is also said: 3,000 years. Ibn Kathir said: this is strange, and stranger than it is what Ibn Asakir said: that it reached me that he lived thirty-six or thirty-two years, and that he was after Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, for that applies only to the second Dhu al-Qarnayn, as we shall mention. I say: likewise what the Imam mentioned of his going to the Children of Israel, arriving at Jerusalem, and slaughtering at its altar, for it can hardly be attributed to the first. There is disagreement about his prophethood, after agreement on his Islam and his guardianship (wilayah). It is said he was a prophet, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾, and it is evident that this includes establishment in religion, whose perfection is through prophethood; and based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave him of every thing a means﴾, and prophethood is among all things; and based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿We said, O Dhu al-Qarnayn﴾, and similar. It is said he was an angel, because Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, heard a man say to another: "O Dhu al-Qarnayn!" He said: "O Allah, forgive! Are you not content to be named after the prophets, that you name yourselves after the angels?" Ibn Kathir said: the correct view is that he was neither a prophet nor an angel, but was a righteous, just king who ruled the regions and subdued their people, both kings and others, and the lands submitted to him, and he was a caller to Allah, Exalted, moving among the creation with complete justice and a supported, victorious authority. Al-Khidr was at the head of his army, in the position of the counselor, who in relation to the king is like the vizier. Al-Azraqi and others mentioned that he embraced Islam at the hands of Abraham the Friend, peace be upon him, and he circumambulated the Ka'bah with him and Isma'il, peace be upon them. It is reported that he performed Hajj on foot, and when Abraham, peace be upon him, heard of his coming, he met him and prayed for him and advised him with counsel. It is said that a horse was brought to him to ride, and he said: "I will not ride in a land where the Friend is." At that, the clouds were subjected to him, and the means were folded up for him, and Abraham, peace be upon him, gave him good news of this. So the clouds would carry him, his armies, and all their equipment whenever they wished to raid a people. Abu al-Tufayl said: Ali, may Allah honor his face, was asked about him: was he a prophet or an angel? He said: "He was neither a prophet nor an angel, but he was a servant who loved Allah and so Allah loved him, and who gave sincere counsel to Allah, so He gave him counsel. The clouds were subjected to him, and the means were extended to him." It has been disputed what the reason for his being called Dhu al-Qarnayn is. It is said: because he reached the two horns of the sun, its east and its west. It is said: because he ruled the Romans and Persians; it is said: the Romans and the Turks. It is said: because there was on his head, or on his crown, something resembling two horns. It is said: because he had two locks of hair. It is said: because the two sides of his head were of copper. It is said: because he called people to Allah, Glorious and Majestic, and he was struck on his right horn and died, then Allah raised him, and he was struck on his left horn and died, then Allah raised him. It is said: because he saw in his dream that he ascended to the heavens and grasped the two horns of the sun. It is said: because two generations passed away in his time. It is said: because light and darkness were subjected to him, so when he traveled, the light guided him from in front of him, and the darkness surrounded him from behind. It is said: he was given this title for his bravery. This is it.

As for the second Dhu al-Qarnayn, Ibn Kathir said: he is Alexander son of Philip son of Misrim son of Harmas son of Maytun son of Rumi son of Lit son of Yunan son of Yafith son of Nunah son of Sharkhun son of Rumiyyah son of Thawnat son of Nufil son of Rumi son of al-Asfar son of al-Anz son of al-Is son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim the Friend, peace be upon them both. Thus did Ibn Asakir, the Macedonian, the Greek, the Egyptian, the founder of Alexandria, by whose days the Romans date their history, trace his lineage. He was far later than the first by a long age of more than two thousand years. This one lived about three hundred years before Christ, peace be upon him. His vizier was Aristotle the philosopher, and he is the one who killed Dara son of Dara, humbled the kings of Persia, and trampled their land. Then Ibn Kathir said: we have clarified this because many people believe that they are one and the same, and that the one mentioned in the Noble Qur'an is this later one, and so a great error and great corruption occur. How could it not be so? The first was a righteous, believing servant and a just king whose vizier was al-Khidr, peace be upon him. It has been said that he was a prophet. As for the second, he was a disbeliever, whose vizier was Aristotle the philosopher, and the time between them is more than two thousand years. How can this be compared to that? End. I say: "al-Maqduni" is a nisba to a town in the lands of the Romans, west of the abode of the Sunni sultanate, Constantinople, protected, may it never cease to be filled with religious rites. Between them is a distance of fifteen days' journey or about that. Near the city of Siruz, whose name in the language of the Greeks is Maqdunia, was the seat of this Alexander's kingdom. Today it is a desolate wasteland where no one lives, but in it are signs that tell of the greatness of its prosperity in the age of its settlement, and the end of the might of its governor and his authority. I passed by it on my return from some of the sultanic campaigns, and I witnessed in it wondrous remains that contain a lesson for those with insight.

﴿Say﴾ to them in reply: ﴿I will recite to you﴾, that is: I will mention to you ﴿from him﴾, that is: from Dhu al-Qarnayn.

﴿A remembrance﴾, that is: a mentioned report. Since this came by way of recited revelation, related from the side of Allah, Glorious and Majestic, it was said: "I will recite," or "I will recite concerning his matter, from His side, a remembrance," that is: a Qur'an. The sin (in sa-atlu) is for emphasis and to indicate the certainty appropriate to the station of his support, peace be upon him, and the confirmation of his fulfillment of the promise; that is, I will absolutely not abandon recitation, as in the words of one who said: "I will thank Amr, if my death is delayed, for favors that were not missed even if they were great." It does not indicate that the recitation will take place in the future, as some have said, because this verse was not revealed on its own before the revelation of the complete story, but connected to what follows, during the period in which they asked him, peace be upon him, about it, and about the Spirit, and about the People of the Cave. He said to them, peace be upon him: "Come to me tomorrow and I will inform you," and revelation was delayed for fifteen days, or forty, as was mentioned earlier. And the saying of the Glorious and Majestic:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 84:

﴿Indeed, We established him in the land.﴾ This begins the recitation of the well-known reminder, just as was promised. Here, al-tamkin (establishment, i.e., empowering and preparing the means) means enabling him and paving the way for causes. It is said: makkanahu and makkana lahu. The meaning of the first is: He made him capable and strong; the meaning of the second is: He gave him capacity and strength. Because the two are concomitant in existence and close in meaning, each is used in the place of the other, as in His words, Exalted and High: ﴿We had established them in the land as We had not established you﴾, meaning: We made them capable, in terms of powers, means and instruments, of various kinds of disposal over it, with the strength and abundance of wealth, and the support of numbers and resources that We had not given you. It is as if it were said: "as We had not established you in it," that is, "as We had not made you capable of that in it," or "We established them in the land as We had not established for you," and so on. If tamkin is taken from makan (place), on the assumption that its mim is original, as was indicated in the surah of Yusuf, peace be upon him, then the meaning is: We gave him a capacity and power to dispose of the land in terms of management, judgment and means, such that the clouds were subjected to him, the means were extended for him, light was spread out for him, night and day were alike to him, travel across the land was made easy for him, and its roads were made smooth for him.

﴿And We gave him of every thing﴾ that he desired of the important matters of his kingdom and the aims connected with his authority.

﴿a means﴾, that is, a way that brings him to it; it is everything by which one reaches the desired goal, whether knowledge, power, or instrument.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 85:

﴿Fa-atbaʿa﴾ with a cut (qat'): that is, he intended to reach the place of sunset, so he followed ﴿a cause (sabab)﴾ that would bring him to it. Perhaps the intention to reach the place of sunset from the outset was in consideration of the solar motion. It is read as (fa-ittaba'a), from the form of (ifti'al), and the difference is that the first carries the meaning of overtaking and hastening, which the second does not.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 86:

﴿Until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun﴾, meaning: the farthest extent of the land towards the west, to the point where no one can pass beyond it. He stood at the edge of the western Encompassing Sea, which is called Uqyanus (Oceanus), in which are the islands called al-Khalidat (the Eternal Isles), which are the starting point of longitudes according to one of the two opinions.

﴿He found it﴾, meaning: the sun.

﴿setting in a murky spring﴾, meaning: possessing ḥama'a, which is black mud, from the expression "hami'at al-bi'r" when its mud became abundant. It was also read as (ḥamiya), meaning: hot. It is narrated that Mu'awiya, may Allah be pleased with him, recited (ḥamiya), and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, was with him and said (ḥami'a). Mu'awiya then said to Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As: "How do you recite it?" He said: "As the Commander of the Faithful recites." Then he directed a question to Ka'b al-Ahbar: "How do you find the sun setting?" He said: "In water and mud," and it is narrated as "in tha'th" (mire). This agreed with the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. There is no definitive contradiction between them, since the spring may combine both descriptions, and the ya' in the second reading may have become a transformed form of the hamza because of the kasra before it. As for Mu'awiya's return to the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, on the basis of what he heard from Ka'b, even though his own recitation is also certainly transmitted, the reason is that the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is definitive in its meaning, while his own is only probable. Perhaps when he reached the shore of the Ocean he saw it that way, since nothing within the range of his sight but water, as the Exalted words ﴿He found it setting﴾ suggest.

﴿And he found near it﴾, near that spring, ﴿a people﴾. It was said: their clothing was the skins of wild beasts, their food was what the sea cast up, and they were disbelievers. Allah, exalted is His remembrance, gave him the choice between punishing them by killing and calling them to faith, and this is the Exalted words: ﴿We said: O Dhu'l-Qarnayn, either you punish﴾ by killing from the very beginning, ﴿or you take among them a good course﴾, meaning: a matter of goodness. This is either by omitting a noun (the word "a course") or by the usage of applying a verbal noun to its subject for emphasis, and this means calling them to Islam, guiding them to the laws. The position of "an" with its clause is either in the nominative, as a subject or as a predicate, or in the accusative, as an object, meaning: either your punishing them is what occurs, or either your command is to punish them, or either you do your punishing. The situation is the same regarding "taking." As for those who do not hold that he was a prophet, they said: that address was conveyed through a prophet of that era, or it was inspiration (ilham) rather than revelation (wahy), since that choice agreed with the law of that prophet.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 87:

﴿He said﴾: that is, Dhu al-Qarnayn, to that prophet, or to those of his close companions who were with him after he had received God's command, choosing the latter alternative.

﴿As for him who does wrong﴾: that is, to himself, and who did not accept my call and persisted in the great wrong he was upon, which is shirk (associating partners with God).

﴿We shall punish him﴾ with killing. It is related from Qatadah that he used to boil those who disbelieved in cauldrons, and whoever believed, he would give him and clothe him.

﴿Then he will be returned to his Lord﴾ in the Hereafter, ﴿and He will punish him﴾ therein ﴿with a terrible punishment﴾, that is, a grievous and dreadful one. This is the punishment of the Fire. In this there is clear evidence that the address was not by way of revelation to him, and that his speech was with the prophet, or with those among his counsellors who were with him.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 18, verse 88:**

﴿As for him who believes﴾ in accordance with My call, ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ as faith requires, ﴿for him will be﴾ in both abodes ﴿a reward, the best [reward]﴾. That is: for him is the best recompense (*mathuba*), or the best deed, or Paradise. *Jaza'an* (as a reward) is either an emphatic infinitive (*masdar mu'akkid*, a verbal noun that reinforces the meaning of the clause), placed before the subject for emphasis, or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "We recompense them with it as a reward." The clause may be circumstantial (*haliyya*), or parenthetical (*mu'taridha*) between the subject and the predicate that precedes it. It may also be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning "recompensed with it," or a specificative accusative (*tamyiz*). It has also been read as *manṣūban* without tanwin (nunation), its tanwin having dropped because of the meeting of two sukun, and as *marfu'an* with tanwin, with *al-husna* in apposition to it and the prepositional phrase as the predicate.

It was said: he was given the choice between killing and capturing [them], and the answer is in the manner of *al-uslub al-hakim* (the wise mode of address, answering in a way other than what is expected), because the apparent [meaning] is to offer them a choice between these two, and they were unbelievers. So He said: as for the unbeliever, the strength of Islam is to be observed regarding him; and as for the believer, he is not to be subjected to anything except what is obligatory. It is also permissible for *imma* ... *wa-amma* to express distribution (*tawzi'*) rather than choice, meaning: let your conduct with them be either punishment or kindness. The first applies to those who remain in their state, and the second to those who repent.

﴿And We shall speak to him of Our command﴾, that is, of what We order, ﴿[as] ease﴾, that is, easy, facilitated, not burdensome. Its implied construction is *dha yusrin* (possessing ease). Or the verbal noun *yusr* is used in its place for emphasis (*mubalaghah*). It has also been read with two dammas (*yusurran*).
Then he followed a way (sababan): that is, a route returning from the west of the sun, leading to its east.

"Until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun" — meaning the place where the sun first rises over the inhabited part of the earth. It is also read with a fatha on the lam (maṭla‘), on the presumption of an elided noun, i.e. "the place of the rising of the sun," since it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It was said: "He found it rising upon a people for whom We had made no shelter against it" — meaning no covering of clothing or building. It was said: they are the Zanj. It is reported from Ka‘b that their land does not hold up buildings, and there are burrows there; when the sun rises they enter the burrows or the sea, and when the day has grown bright they come out to their livelihoods. It is also reported from one of them: "I set out until I passed China, and I asked about these people. They said: between you and them is a journey of a day and a night. So I reached them, and one of them was spreading his ear and wearing the other, and with me was a companion who knew their language. They said to him: 'Have you come to see how the sun rises?' He said: While we were like that, we heard a sound like a clattering, and I fainted; then I came to, and they were rubbing me with oil. When the sun rose over the water, it was above the water like olive oil, so they put us into one of their burrows; when the day had grown bright they came out to the sea to hunt fish, and they threw it in the sun, and it cooked for them." It is also reported from Mujahid: those of the Sudan who do not wear clothing at the rising of the sun are more numerous than all the people of the earth.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 91:**

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., the matter of Dhu al-Qarnayn is as We have described it to you, in the loftiness of his station and the breadth of his dominion. Or, his matter among them is like his matter among the people of the west, in terms of giving them choice and option. It is permissible for it (the word "thus") to be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar) for "he found" (wajada) or "we shall make" (naj'alu), or an adjective of a people, meaning: over a people like that tribe over whom the sun sets, in disbelief and in judgment; or (an adjective of) a covering like your covering of clothing, shelters, mountains, and other than that.

﴿And We had encompassed what was with him﴾ of the means, the numbers, and the equipment, ﴿in full knowledge﴾. It means: that is, [his forces were] of such abundance that none can encompass it except the knowledge of the Subtle, the All-Aware. This is according to the first interpretation. As for the remaining interpretations, what is meant by "what was with him" is that which encompasses what befell him, what proceeded from him, and what he encountered, so reflect.
Then he followed a way (sababan). That is: a third route, lying across between the east and the west, taking its course from the south toward the north.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 93:

﴿Until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾ — between the two mountains that he blocked off between them. This is the furthest end of the land of the Turks on the eastern side, not the two mountains of Armenia and Adharbayjan, as has been imagined. It is also read with a ḍamma (بِالضَّمِّ, i.e., as "السُّدُّ" with a ḍamma on the first letter, with the meaning of barrier built by Allah). It is said: whatever is from the creation of Allah the Exalted is read with a ḍamma, and whatever is from the work of creatures is read with a fatḥa. The accusative of "bayna" (بَيْنَ) is as a direct object, because it is "mablūgh" (reached). It is one of the adverbs (ẓurūf, i.e., words indicating place and time) that are also used as nouns, as it is raised in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Certainly your bond has been severed (laqad taqaṭṭaʿa baynakum)﴾, and it is put in the genitive in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿This is the parting between me and you (hādhā firāqu baynī wa baynik)﴾.

﴿He found beside them﴾ — meaning: behind them, passing beyond them — ﴿a people﴾, meaning: a nation of people.

﴿who scarcely could understand any speech﴾ — because of the strangeness of their language and the dullness of their understanding. It is also read from the form of "if'āl" (yuf'iluna), meaning: they do not make the listener understand their speech. They differed concerning which of the peoples they were. Ḍaḥḥāk said: they are a generation of the Turks. Suddī said: the Turks are a detachment of Yajuj and Majuj, who came out, and Dhu al-Qarnayn built the barrier, so they remained outside it, and all the Turks are from them. It is related from Qatada that they are twenty-two tribes; Dhu al-Qarnayn blocked twenty-one tribes of them, and one tribe remained, so they were named "the Turks" because they were left (turikū) outside. The historians said: the sons of Noah, peace be upon him, are three: Sam, Ham and Yafith. Sam is the father of the Arabs, the non-Arabs and the Romans; Ham is the father of the Abyssinians, the Zanj and the Nubians; and Yafith is the father of the Turks, the Khazars, the Slavs, Yajuj and Majuj.

Qur'anic quotations: translated plainly inside ﴿ ﴾.

"They said" – i.e., through their interpreter, or directly, on the basis that Dhu al-Qarnayn understood their speech, and the conveying of his speech to them was among what God Most High had granted him of the means (asbab).

﴿O Dhu al-Qarnayn, indeed Ya'juj and Ma'juj﴾ – We have mentioned that they are from the descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh, upon him be peace. It is also said: Ya'juj are from the Turks and Ma'juj from the Jil. Their attributes have been disputed. It is said: they are of extremely small body and short stature, their height not exceeding one span. It is said: they are of extreme bulk of body and great height, their stature reaching about one hundred and twenty cubits, and among them are those whose breadth is likewise. It is said: they have claws and molar teeth like those of beasts of prey. Both are non-Arabic names, as evidenced by their being diptote (not declined with tanwin). It is said: they are Arabic, from ajja (أجَّ), meaning the ostrich (al-zalim) ran swiftly, and their original form has a hamza, as Asim recited. It has also been recited without a hamza, and their being diptote is due to definiteness and femininity.

﴿corrupting in the earth﴾ – i.e., in our land, by killing, destruction, and the ruining of crops. It is said: they would go out in the days of spring and leave no green thing without eating it, nor any dry thing without carrying it off. It is also said: they would also eat people.

﴿So shall we make for you a tribute (kharj)﴾ – i.e., a payment (ju'l) from our wealth. The "fa'" (so) is for deriving the offer from their corruption in the earth. It has been recited as (kharaj), and both are one in meaning, like nawl and nawal. It is said: kharaj is what is levied on land and on the protected status (dhimma), while kharj is the verbal noun. It is said: kharj is what is levied on each head, and kharaj is what is levied on the country. It is said: kharj is what you give voluntarily, and kharaj is what is obligatory for you to pay.

﴿on condition that you make a barrier between us and them﴾ – It has also been recited with a dammah (suddan, سُدًّا as sudda).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 95:

﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better"⦁ — with idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters). It is also read with fakk (separation of the two letters), i.e., "ma makkanani" (what has established me).

﴿in which my Lord has established me﴾ and made me firmly established, able, in regard to kingship, wealth, and all other means.

﴿is better﴾ i.e., better than what you wish to give me of tribute (kharj), so I have no need of it.

﴿So help me with strength﴾ i.e., with workmen and craftsmen who excel in building and labor, and with the tools necessary for construction. The "fa" (so) indicates that the command to help is a consequence of the excellence of what God Most High has established him in, of their wealth, or of the non-acceptance of their tribute.

﴿I will set﴾ is the answer to the imperative ﴿between you and them﴾. The placing of the prepositional phrase "between you" before its attachment to the pronoun of Gog and Magog serves to show full concern for their interests, just as they observed this in their saying "between us and them."

﴿a barrier﴾ i.e., a strong barrier and a firm rampart. It is greater than a dam (sadd) and more secure. It is said: "a garment that is mudarram," meaning it has patches upon patches. This is a fulfilment of their aim beyond what they were hoping for.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 96:

﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾. It is the plural of *zubrah* (a large piece), like *ghuraf* for *ghurfah*. This does not conflict with the return of their tribute, because what was commanded is the giving of the price, or the handing over. This is indicated by the recitation with the hamza connected (*wasl*), meaning: "Bring me blocks of iron," with the preposition *ba'* omitted, as in *amartuka al-khayr* ("I commanded you the good"). Also, giving the tool is a form of help with strength, not a tribute for the work. Perhaps the command was specifically to give these (iron blocks) and not other tools such as rocks and firewood and the like, because the need for them is more pressing, since they are the pillar of the dam, and their availability is rarer. It is said that he dug for the foundation until he reached water, and made the foundation of rock and molten copper, and the structure of blocks of iron with firewood and charcoal between them, until he closed the gap between the two mountains up to their peaks, which was a hundred farsakhs. This is the meaning of His saying, Mighty is He, ﴿until, when he had levelled between the two cliffs﴾, that is: they brought them to him, and he began to build bit by bit until, when he made the building between the two sides of the mountains level with them (p-246) in height, according to the described manner. It is said that its height was two hundred cubits and its width fifty cubits. It was read *sawwa* (from *taswiyah*) and *suwwiya* (in the passive voice). ﴿He said﴾, to the workers, ﴿Blow﴾, that is: with the bellows on the iron that was built, so they did. ﴿Until, when he had made it﴾, that is: the thing blown upon,

﴿fire﴾, that is: like fire in heat and appearance. Attributing the making mentioned to Dhu al-Qarnayn, although it is the act of the workers, is to draw attention to the fact that he is the principal in this, and they are in the position of the tool. ﴿He said﴾ to those who take charge of the copper, from melting and the like,

﴿Bring me, I will pour over it molten copper﴾, that is: bring me *qitran*, that is: molten copper. *Ufrigh 'alayhi qitran* ("I will pour over it molten copper"), where the first (verb) is omitted because the second indicates it. It was also read with *wasl*. That is: bring me, as if he were summoning them to help with the hand at the time of pouring. Attributing the pouring to himself is for the secret upon which you have just paused, and likewise the discussion regarding His saying, Exalted is He, "*sawwa*" and His saying "*aj'al*."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 97:

﴿So they were not able﴾ with the deletion of the tā' of the iftiʿāl form (ta'ammul: the reflexive infixed t) for lightening, and to avoid the meeting of two similar letters (al-mutaqāribayn). It is also read with idghām (assimilation). In this there is a gathering of two unvowelled letters (al-sākinayn) in a non-standard way. It is also read with the sīn being changed into ṣād. The "fā'" is eloquent (faṣīḥah), meaning: they did what they were commanded regarding bringing the molten copper (al-qiṭr), or the bringing; so he poured it over it, and it mixed and some of it stuck to some other, and it became a solid mountain (jabalan ṣaldan). Then Yājūj and Mājūj came, intending to climb over it and to dig through it, but they were not able ﴿to make it manifest﴾, meaning: to climb over it and ascend upon it, because of its height and smoothness.

﴿And they were not able to make a breach in it﴾ because of its hardness and thickness. This is a great miracle, for when those many layers are affected by the heat of the fire, no living creature is able to come near them, let alone blow into them until they become like fire, or pour molten copper over them. It is as if He, glory be to Him and exalted, diverted the effect of that great heat away from the bodies of those who were working on the construction, so that what happened happened, and God is powerful over all things. It has also been said that he built it from rocks linked to one another with clamps (kalālīb) of iron and copper, melted into its hollows, such that no gap remained there at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 98:

﴿He said﴾ That is, Dhu al-Qarnayn, to those among the people of that land who were with him, and others. ﴿This﴾ refers to the barrier (sadd). It was also said: it refers to his being empowered to build it, and the favour belongs to the one who comes first. That is: this which has appeared at my hands and has come about through my own effort, namely the barrier, whose nature is what has been mentioned of solidity and difficulty of access.

﴿a mercy﴾ That is, the effect of a great mercy, expressed by it as an intensification, ﴿from my Lord﴾ upon all of His servants, and especially upon its neighbours. In this there is a notification that it is not of the kind of effects that normally arise from the effort of creatures, but is rather a purely divine benevolence, even though it appeared through my effort. The mention of the attribute of lordship (rubūbiyyah) is to nurture the meaning of mercy.

﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes﴾ is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ūl), and it refers to the Day of Resurrection, not the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj as has been said. For the noble composition does not support that. The meaning of its coming is what encompasses its coming and the coming of its precursors, among them their emergence, the emergence of the Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa (peace be upon him), and the like. Not merely the imminence of its occurrence, as has been said, for some of the matters that will be related occur after its coming, definitely.

﴿He will make it﴾ That is, the barrier referred to, along with its solidity and firmness. In it there is a grandeur that is not found in directing the previous reference to the aforementioned empowerment. ﴿level (dakkā')﴾ That is, a levelled land. It was read as (dakkan), meaning crushed and levelled with the ground. Everything that spreads out after being raised has become levelled (indakka), and from this comes the camel that is adakk, that is, one whose hump is flattened. This making takes place at the time the promise comes, with the coming of some of its precursors. In it is an explanation of the greatness of His power, the Mighty and Majestic, after the explanation of the vastness of His mercy.

﴿And the promise of my Lord is ever true﴾ That is, His known promise, or everything He has promised, so that this enters into it primarily.

﴿true﴾ Established without doubt, certainly occurring without fail. This sentence is a concluding remark from Dhu al-Qarnayn regarding what he mentioned of the conditional sentence, and an affirmation and confirmation of its content, and it is the last of what is related of his story. And the saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 99:**

﴿And We left some of them﴾: this is a statement delivered from His presence, exalted be He, conjoined with His saying, exalted be He, "He made it level (ja'alahu dakka')," and it confirms its meaning. That is, We made some of the creatures [go forth in confusion].

﴿On that day﴾: that is, on the day when the promise came with the arrival of some of its beginnings, ﴿surging against one another﴾, that is, some others of them, who will be agitated like the surging of the waves of the sea, and their humans and jinn will be mixed together, bewildered from the severity of the terror. Perhaps this is before the first blast. Or [the meaning is]: We left some of Gog and Magog, who surge against some others of them when they come out from the barrier, crowding into the lands.

It is narrated that they will come to the sea and drink its water and eat its creatures, then they will eat the trees, and whoever of the people who did not fortify themselves they overpower. They will not be able to reach Mecca, Medina and Bayt al-Maqdis. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, will send a worm (naghaf) into their necks, and it will enter their ears, and they will die the death of a single soul. Then Allah, exalted be He, will send birds upon them, which will throw them into the sea. Then He will send rain that washes the earth and purifies it of their stench, until He leaves it like a mirror (zalfa), and then blessing will be placed in it. This will be after the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the killing of the Dajjal.

﴿And the Trumpet will be blown﴾: this is the second blast, by the requirement of the fa' (then) in His saying, exalted be He, ﴿then We will gather them﴾. Perhaps the non-mention of the first blast is because it is a general calamity in which there is no state specific to the disbelievers, and so that there is no separation between what occurs in the first creation of the states and terrors and what occurs in the later creation. That is, We gathered the creatures after their joints had been scattered and their bodies torn apart, into one plain, for reckoning and recompense.

﴿A gathering﴾: that is, a wondrous gathering whose true nature cannot be comprehended.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 100:

﴿And We will present Hell﴾ — i.e., We will make it manifest and bring it forth — ﴿on that Day﴾ — i.e., the Day when We gather all of creation together.

﴿to the disbelievers﴾ — from among them — since We will place it in a position where they can see it, and they will hear its raging (taghayyuz) and roaring (zafir).

﴿a presentation﴾ — i.e., a dreadful, terrifying presentation whose extent cannot be measured. The specification of the presentation to them, although it is in view of all who are assembled, is because it is for their sake alone.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 101:

﴿Those whose eyes were﴾ in this world ﴿in a covering﴾ thick, and a heavy veil encompassing them on every side.

﴿from My remembrance﴾ from the signs that lead people of insight, who reflect upon them, to remember Me through affirming My oneness and glorifying Me; or their insight-eyes were under a covering from My remembrance in a manner befitting My station; or from the Noble Qur'an. ﴿And they were﴾ moreover ﴿unable to hear﴾ because of the extreme deafness to the truth and the complete hostility toward the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿hearing﴾ listening to My remembrance and My true words, which falsehood cannot reach from before it or from behind it. This is an illustration of their turning away from the auditory proofs, just as the first (clause) is a depiction of their blindness to the signs witnessed by sight. The relative pronoun is an attribute of the disbelievers, or a substitute for them, or an explanation. It was brought to censure them by what is within the scope of the relative clause, and to indicate that it is the cause of what befell them of the exposure of Hell to them (p-248), for that is only because they did not employ their faculties regarding the signs that presented themselves to them in the world, and turned away from them, although they were means of salvation from what they were tried with in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 102:

﴿Do those who disbelieve think﴾ i.e., who disbelieved in Me, as His saying "My servants" indicates. Al-husban (reckoning) means al-zann (supposition). It has also been read: (afa-zanna) and the hamza is for denial and reproach, in the sense of denying and finding repugnant what has occurred, just as in your saying: "Did you strike your father?" — not denying that it happened, as in his saying: "Shall I strike my father?" The fa' is for coordination with an implied element that the relative clause makes explicit, directing the denial and reproach at both conjoined elements together, as when the coordinated element is assumed to be negated in His saying, "Will you not then reason?" (afa-la ta'qilun), meaning: "Do you not hear and so do not reason?" — not only at the conjoined element, as when it is assumed to be affirmative, meaning: "Do you hear and so do not reason?" The meaning is: Did they disbelieve in Me despite My exalted station, and so reckon ﴿that they could take My servants as protectors apart from Me﴾ — among the angels, Jesus, and Ezra, peace be upon them. And they are under My dominion and sovereignty.

﴿protectors﴾ — worshipped deities who would help them against My might. What has been said, that it is coordinated with what precedes it in His saying, "were ... etc." and "and they were ... etc.", indicating that the reckoning arises from blindness and deafness, and that the hamza of denial has been placed before it as censure upon censure and to cut it off from the elements conjoined to it in wording but not in meaning, in order to signal independent emphasis on the censure — which the omission of the pronoun and the mention of an attribute other than blindness and deafness refuse — and that these two are presented as their innate states, and they are not mentioned as voluntary acts such as their reckoning, so that it would be apt to derive it from them. Moreover, it is an ancient religion for them, and it is not possible to make it arise from their deafness to the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and restricting the denial to their reckoning, which comes after that, is a forced interpretation that is plain. What is within the scope of the relative clause of "an" serves in place of the two objects of "hasiba," as in His saying: ﴿And they reckoned that there would be no trial﴾, meaning: "Do they reckon that they take them as protectors?" in the sense that this is not taking at all, since taking is only from both sides, and they, upon them be prayer and peace, are exalted above being their protectors at all, by their saying: ﴿Glory be to You, You are our protector, not them﴾. It has also been said: its second object is omitted, meaning: "Do they reckon their taking them to be beneficial to them?" The first view is the correct one, because in this there is a concession to the taking itself and a regarding of it in general.

It has been read: (afa-hasbu) those who disbelieve, meaning: "Is it then enough for them, sufficient for them, that they take them as protectors?" — as a nominal sentence with subject and predicate, or as a verb with its agent; for when the adjective takes the hamza, it equals the verb in government, and the hamza is then for the denial of occurrence.

﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell﴾ — i.e., readied it ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, the known ones. He turned away from the pronoun to censure them and to indicate that this preparation is due to their disbelief, which includes their false reckoning.

﴿as a welcome﴾ — i.e., something by which they enjoy themselves upon arrival, which is what is prepared for a guest, that is, the visitor, of the food that is present. In this there is a rebuke of them for their reckoning and a mockery of them, since their taking those beings as protectors was of the same kind as preparing equipment and provisions for the Day of Return. So it is as if it were said: We have readied for them, in place of what they prepared for themselves of equipment and store, Hell as equipment. In mentioning the welcome there is an allusion that, beyond Hell, they have punishments of which this is a model. It has also been said: the nuzul is the place of descent, and for this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, explained it as "the abode."

Say: "Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in respect of their deeds?"

The second address, "Say," is directed at the disbelievers, in the mode of rebuke (al-tawbikh). The use of the first-person plural in "We inform" (nunabbi'ukum) is to specify them from the outset, and to indicate that the news is also known to the believers. As for "the greatest losers in respect of their deeds" (bi-l-akhsarina a'mala), the accusative here is a tamyiz (specification). The plural form of "deeds" (a'mal) indicates the variety of these deeds.

This is an explanation of the state of the disbelievers with regard to the good deeds that proceeded from them, which are good in themselves and also in their own reckoning, since they were pleased with them, confident of receiving their reward, and seeing their effects. Following this, it explains their state with regard to their evil deeds, which are evil in themselves while appearing good in their own reckoning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 104:

﴿Those whose effort has gone astray﴾ in establishing those deeds, i.e., it was lost and became entirely void.

﴿in the life of this world﴾ is related to "effort," not to "gone astray," because the nullification of their effort is not restricted to this world. It has been said: the intended people are the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitab), so said Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with them. In that case, what they did of the abrogated rulings (al-ahkam al-mansukha, i.e., rulings superseded by later revelation) concerning acts of worship (al-'ibadat) is included among the deeds. It has also been said: they are the monks (al-rahabina) who confine themselves in monasteries (al-sawami') and subject themselves to severe ascetic exercises; and perhaps it encompasses them and others among the disbelievers. The relative clause (al-mawsul) is in the nominative case, being the predicate of an omitted subject, since it is the answer to a question, as if it were said: "Who are they?" So it was said: "Those who..." etc. Making it genitive, as an attribute of "the greatest losers" (al-akhsarin), or as an apposition to it, or accusative by way of dispraise (al-dhamm), with the answer being what follows in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those are...﴾ ... the verse, is rejected, because its opening does not indicate the loss of deeds and the going astray of effort, as the context of the answer requires. The first branching, although it indicates their nullification, is silent about what is central in realizing the meaning of loss: the certainty of obtaining profit and the belief that benefit lies in what they did. Moreover, the second branching definitively removes this possibility entirely, since there is no room to include it under the command given the majestic plural (nun al-'azamah).

﴿while they think they are doing good works﴾ Ihsan (excellence) is performing deeds in the proper manner, and it is their descriptive goodness, which entails their intrinsic goodness. That is, they think that they are doing that in the proper manner, and this is due to their admiration for their deeds, which they strove to establish and endured hardship to accomplish. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "gone astray," i.e., their aforementioned effort was lost, while the state is that they think they are excelling in that and benefiting from its effects. Or it is from the genitive noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) because it is in the nominative position, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾, i.e., their effort was lost. The circumstantial clause "that they..." etc. The difference between the two is that what accompanies the state of their aforementioned thinking in the first is the going astray of their effort, and in the second it is their effort itself. The first is more suited to explaining their error.

**"Those"** is a resumptive statement from Him, exalted is He, which is sequenced to complete the description of the greatest losers, to clarify the cause of their loss and the misguidance of their effort, and to identify them so that the description applies to the addressees without being included in the command. That is: "those" who are described by what was mentioned of the misguidance of effort together with the aforementioned reckoning.

﴿**who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord**﴾ — in His proofs calling to **tawhid** (the affirmation of God's oneness) by reason (**'aql**) and by transmitted textual evidence (**naql**). The mention of the title of **lordship** (rubūbiyyah) serves to increase the reprehensibility of their state in the aforementioned disbelief.

﴿**and in His meeting**﴾ — with resurrection and what follows it of the matters of the Hereafter, as they really are.

﴿**so their deeds are nullified**﴾ — because of that, the well-known deeds (**a'mal**) are nullified completely (**ḥubūṭan kulliyyan**).

﴿**so We shall not assign to them**﴾ — that is, to those described by what has passed of the nullification of deeds. It is also read with the **yā'** (i.e., "He shall not assign").

﴿**any weight on the Day of Resurrection**﴾ — that is, We shall disdain them, and We shall not give them any measure or consideration, because the basis of that is good deeds, and these have been nullified entirely. Since this disdain is among the consequences of the nullification of deeds, it is joined to it by way of consequence. As for what is among the requitals of disbelief, it will come after this. Or: We shall not set up a scale on account of the weighing of their deeds; for it is set up only for the people of good and bad deeds among the monotheists, so that by it the measures of acts of obedience and of sins may be distinguished, so that expiation or its absence may follow from it. For among the monotheists this takes place by way of quantity; but as for disbelief, its nullifying of good deeds is according to quality, not quantity, so a scale is certainly not set up for them.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 106:

"That" is an explanation of the outcome of their disbelief and all their other sins, following the explanation of the outcome of their deeds that were rendered void by it; that is, the matter is that. And the words of Him, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Their recompense is Hell﴾ form a sentence explaining it. Or "That" is a subject (mubtada'), the sentence is its predicate (khabar), and the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is omitted; that is, their recompense is by it, or their recompense is in its place. And Jahannam is its predicate. Or "their recompense" is its predicate and Jahannam is an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) to the predicate.

﴿Because they disbelieved﴾ is a clear statement that what was mentioned is the recompense for their disbelief, which encompasses all the other ugly deeds indicated by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and they took My signs and My messengers in mockery﴾, that is, made a mockery of them both. For they were not content with mere disbelief in the signs and the messengers, but also committed the like of that great offense.

**(Tafsir of Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on Surah 18, verse 107)**

﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ is an exposition, by way of promise, of the final destiny of those who possessed the opposites of what the disbelievers possessed, following the exposition of the disbelievers' destiny by way of warning; that is, they believed in the signs of their Lord and in meeting Him.

﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ from among the deeds, ﴿there will be for them﴾ in what preceded of the decree of Allah the Exalted and His promise. In this there is an allusion that the effect of mercy reaches them in accordance with the eternal compassion, unlike what passed concerning the making of Jahannam a place of lodging (nuzul) for the disbelievers, since that is in accordance with what arose from their evil choice.

﴿Gardens of Firdaws﴾. It is reported from Mujahid that al-Firdaws is the orchard, in the Byzantine (Rumi) language. ʿIkrimah said: it is the garden in the Abyssinian language. al-Dahhak said: it is the garden with densely interwoven trees. It was said: it is the garden that produces various kinds of plants. It was said: it is the garden of vines specifically. It was said: it is that whose majority is vines. al-Mubarrad said: it is, as I have heard from the Arabs, densely interwoven trees, and most often these are of grapes. It is reported from Ka'b that there is no garden higher than the Garden of Firdaws, and in it are those who enjoin good and forbid evil. And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "In Paradise there are one hundred degrees, between each degree is a distance of one hundred years, and al-Firdaws is the highest of them, and from it the four rivers flow. So when you ask Allah the Exalted, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth."

﴿Nuzulan﴾ is the predicate of "kanat" (were), and the prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element, either as a circumstantial clause (hal) of "nuzulan," or as an explanation (bayan), or as a circumstantial clause of "Gardens of Firdaws." The predicate is the prepositional phrase. If nuzul is taken to mean what is prepared for the one who alights, then the meaning is: the fruits of the Gardens of Firdaws were for them a nuzul, or the Gardens themselves were made a nuzul, as an intensification in honour. In this there is a notification that they, in what Allah has prepared for them, according to what was related upon the tongue of prophethood in His saying: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived," stands in the position of a nuzul relative to a feast of hospitality. If it is taken to mean a dwelling-place (manzil), then the meaning is evident.

(p-251) ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿They will not desire any removal from it﴾ — ḥiwal is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like ʿiwaj and ṣighar; that is, they will not seek any transference away from it, since it is inconceivable that there should be anything more precious to them and more exalted than it, such that their souls would strive toward it or their eyes would aspire to it. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is the negation of transference and the emphasis on eternal abiding. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) either from the subject of khālidīna (the word "abiding") or from the pronoun within it, in which case it is a nested circumstantial clause (ḥāl mutadākhilah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 18, verse 109:

﴿Say: Even if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾, i.e., the kind of sea (jins al-bahr), ﴿ink﴾ (midad), which is what the inkwell is supplied with of ink (hibr), ﴿for the words of my Lord﴾ to transcribe the words of His knowledge and His wisdom, of which is included what has been mentioned of the signs calling to monotheism and warning against associating partners with Him.

﴿the sea would be exhausted﴾ despite its abundance, and nothing of it would remain, because it is finite (li-tanahihi).

﴿before the words of my Lord are exhausted﴾ It has also been read with the letter ya' (yanfada), and the meaning is: without the words of my Lord being exhausted. Because they are not finite, the statement gives no indication that they would be exhausted after the sea is exhausted. In the attribution of "words" to the name of the Lord, attributed to His pronoun ﷺ in both places, there is an unmistakable exaltation of the attributed and an honouring of the one to whom it is attributed. The explicit mention of "sea" and "words" in place of a pronoun is for the sake of greater affirmation.

﴿And if We were to bring﴾ is a statement from the side of the Exalted, not included in the words taught (al-kalam al-mulaqqan), brought to confirm its content and to attest its meaning, with added exaggeration and emphasis. The "wa" (waw) is for conjoining the clause to its counterpart which is a resumptive clause (al-mustanifa) opposite to it, which has been elided because the mentioned clause clearly indicates it, meaning: the sea would be exhausted without the words of Him, exalted, being exhausted, even if We were not to bring the like of it as ink, and even if We were to bring it by Our overwhelming power.

﴿with the like of it as a supply﴾ (madadan), as aid and addition; because the collection of two finite things is finite, rather the collection of everything that enters existence of bodies can only be finite, due to the decisive proofs establishing the finitude of dimensions. It has also been read: (midadan), the plural of mudda, which is what the scribe draws upon, and it has been read: (midadan).

﴿Say﴾ to them, after you have explained to them the matter of His words, exalted is He: ﴿I am only a human being like you﴾, not claiming to encompass His perfect words.

﴿It is revealed to me﴾ from those words ﴿that your God is one God﴾, having no partner in creation or in the rest of the rulings of divinity. It is only in this that I am distinguished from you.

﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾: ''raja'' (hope) is the expectation of attaining good in the future. By ''meeting Him'', exalted is He, is meant His honor (karamah). The use of the past tense (''kana'') with the future sense indicates that what befits the believer's state is continuity and persistence in hoping for the meeting, meaning: whoever persists in hoping for His honor, exalted is He.

﴿let him do﴾ in order to attain that noble aim ﴿righteous deeds﴾ in themselves, befitting that which is hoped for, as those who believed and did righteous deeds did.

﴿and let him not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾, neither overt association (''shirk jali''), as those who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in His meeting did, nor hidden association (''shirk khafi''), as those who show off (ahl al-riya') do, and whoever seeks a reward by it. The preference for placing the explicit noun (''al-muzhar'') in place of the pronoun (''al-mudmar'') in both places, together with mention of the title of lordship (''al-rububiyya''), serves to increase confirmation and to indicate that the title is the reason for the command and prohibition, and for the obligation to comply, both in doing and in refraining.

It is narrated that Jundub ibn Zuhayr (may Allah be pleased with him) said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I do an action for the sake of Allah, exalted is He, but when it is seen, it pleases me." He (ﷺ) said: "Allah does not accept what is associated with another in it." So this verse was revealed confirming his words.

It is also narrated that he (ﷺ) said to him: "You will have two rewards: the reward of the secret and the reward of the open, and that is when he intends that he be followed as an example."

And from him (ﷺ): "Beware of the lesser shirk." It was said: "What is the lesser shirk?" He said: "Riya' (showing off)."

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Kahf from its end, it will be a light for him from his forehead to his feet, and whoever recites it entirely, it will be a light for him from the earth to the sky."

And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites at his bed: ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you, it is revealed to me﴾ ... etc., his bed will become a light shining as far as Makkah, filled with that light are angels who send blessings upon him until he rises. And if his bed is in Makkah, it will be a light shining from his bed to the Bayt al-Ma'mur, filled with that light are angels who send blessings upon him until he wakes up."

All praise is due to Allah, glorified is He, for His great blessings.
